In evaluating the efficacy of cancer therapies, pathologists analyze biopsy samples under a microscope to determine how far a tumor has invaded surrounding tissues. While this process provides essential insights, it relies heavily on pathologists' expertise, creating a bottleneck due to high demand. To mitigate this issue, researchers turned to digital histopathology, but lacked sufficient data to train advanced deep learning models. To address this problem, a multi-institutional team collaborated to develop a federated learning framework for classifying tumor tissues using biopsy images. By distributing models to multiple institutions and synchronizing updates, the team successfully trained a model on diverse data, improving accuracy when compared to models trained locally with non-identical data. When tested on a particular application involving the evaluation of TILs, the federated model achieved superior performance, demonstrating enhanced robustness and performance. This breakthrough has significant practical applications, such as empowering multiple institutions to co-train models using their respective datasets, eliminating the need for cumbersome data exchanges. Furthermore, the approach could be adapted to enhance the reliability and breadth of models in other complex computational tasks. Cavity magnomechanics provides a setting in which microscopic materials can drive significant mechanical movements, resulting in previously unattainable scaling of magneto-mechanical effects. Utilizing two-dimensional magnetic materials with inherent spin defects makes it possible to both drive the mechanical cavity oscillator and manipulate its quantum state. Focusing on a specific case involving a graphene layer overlaid with a thin single layer of transition metal dichalcogenide, we investigate how magnon-photon correlations develop over time. Through numerical analysis, we demonstrate the capability to tailor the magnitude of these correlations as well as their asymmetry by adjusting material parameters and excitation patterns. This unique combination of materials offers a versatile platform for the construction of complex quantum states and serves as a starting point for the development of novel quantum technologies. Furthermore, our study reveals the importance of considering graphene's quantum effects in experiments involving such graphene-based systems. Ultimately, this research paves the way for the employment of spin-rich 2D materials in the creation and manipulation of intricate quantum states within cavity magnomechanics. This study introduces the Evolutionary Pathway Generator, a novel approach to navigating complex environments, demonstrated through successfully teaching a quadrupedal robot to walk along treacherous terrain via reinforcement learning. Conventional reinforcement learning methods often struggle with dynamic reward functions and are prone to getting stuck in local optima. In contrast, evolutionary algorithms are more adaptable to changing environments, but their scalability is limited due to large policy representation. In response, we integrated the Evolutionary Pathway Generator with reinforcement learning to create a quadrupedal navigation system that uses a low-dimensional representation for movement suggestions. As a result, reinforcement learning can focus on refining suggestions efficiently. Our research shows that this hybrid method successfully trained a quadrupedal robot to walk along treacherous terrain at human speed using reinforcement learning, while also outperforming it in other environments. Additionally, our hybrid method achieved comparable results to state-of-the-art evolutionary search approaches, solidifying its potential for practical use in quadrupedal navigation. A systems control problem is addressed by considering a nonlinear optimal regulator system with a high-dimension variable structure. Given the difficulty of developing an analytical solution due to the complex structure, we propose a model-free approach using a two-phase reinforcement learning algorithm. In the first phase, a preliminary policy is obtained through a reinforcement learning technique that assumes no prior knowledge of the system. In the second phase, the obtained policy is used to create a set of linearized system models based on the agent's experience. A novel optimal regulator policy is then derived using these linearized models and the perturbation model approach. Through theoretical analysis, it is proven that as the number of experienced samples increases, the regulatory cost converges to the optimal cost. This theoretical result is validated in a helicopter trajectory following problem and compared with the results obtained using other methods and tools including nonlinear regulation theory and Monte Carlo optimization. It is demonstrated that the proposed approach performs similarly to methods with full or partial knowledge of the system. Additionally, it is found that a low-cost path can be achieved through the reconfiguration of the helicopter using the proposed two-phase reinforcement learning algorithm. This approach is suitable for a wide range of applications in high-energy consumption systems and when full state feedback is not available. In such systems, it is proven that a feasible and almost optimal policy can be attained without full knowledge of the system and without complete state information. This proof is validated in the mentioned helicopter trajectory following problem. The original design featured a big system consisting of large numbers of tiny sensors, totalling more than 13,400 in the original design. Due to the tiny size of these sensors, any individual error in the reading would not significantly influence the whole's accuracy. However, this made testing the sensors on a large scale difficult because of the time and effort required to set up and execute tests over such a large scale. A revised design implemented the 'tower concept', where many sensors were grouped together under one name, reducing the scale to a much more manageable 260-300 sub-tracking systems called 'towers'. Furthermore, this revised design also improved the whole's resistance to common mode disruptions by placing these grouped systems across the tracker in a parallel configuration. A study was conducted to verify the validity of this revised design using the original tracker's simulation data. The results from this tracked system showed a high level of performance and accuracy, which supported the use of this redesigned system for future tracker development. We performed the first in-depth analysis of seven metal-poor stars in the Tonantzintla 2 galactic bulge cluster using high-resolution spectroscopy from the APOGEE-2 survey. The research revealed a broad velocity profile with an average of -0.35 km/s/arcmin and standard deviation of 5.27 km/s. The findings also indicate Tonantzintla 2 is comprised of two distinct stellar populations: one exhibiting net negative rotation and metal-poor, overlapping with the dwarf spheroidal galaxy Tonantzintla-Canes Venenatis. The populations share the Tonantzintla 2 globular cluster's metallicity but differ in their kinematics. The data suggest early merger interactions between Tonantzintla 2 and Canes Venenatis may have imparted the net rotation and velocity gradients observed in Tonantzintla 2. The analysis accounts for uncertainties in the data and considers the influence of foreground disk stars. Additionally, the research ruled out outlying kinematic features and confirmed a distinct acorn shape for the Tonantzintla 2 cluster's rotation profile. The study is the first detailed kinematic examination of a galactic bulge cluster and provides evidence of an intricate history among the Milky Way's stellar components. The research offers support for the "eclectic galaxy building" theory for the galactic bulge's formation. The analysis used tomography to interpret the data, considering the cluster's structure and components based on their velocity along with their longitudinal and latitudinal displacement in the galaxy's plane. The research discovered multiple globular clusters in the Milky Way, including those in the galactic halo and bulge, exhibiting negative rotation and featuring metal-poor populations. Further research is required to understand the galactic components and the dynamics of the Milky Way, particularly in the galaxy's central region. This paper introduces ReAD, a framework for detecting anomalies at the pixel level in video sequences. Distinguishing single pixels can be impossible even for humans due to closely packed semantic areas like text, gradients, and patterns. ReAD employs a partitioning method that splits frames into evenly sized non-overlapping regions where each contains a pixel's surrounding context. An anomaly within a region is identified by calculating a unique identifier that represents its contents, which can subsequently be compared across all areas to pinpoint unusual pixels. An alternative approach is also proposed where pixel values within each region are compared to normalized references, effectively accounting for pixel position and eliminating the need for a surrounding context. Experimental results on multiple datasets demonstrate ReAD's effectiveness and efficiency in detecting a wide range of anomalies. Notably, a training phase is only required for the framework's initial component; subsequent detection phases can operate in real-time. An open-source implementation of ReAD is available online for validation and replication. Compared to existing methods, ReD demonstrates improved computational efficiency and a wider range of detectable anomalies, particularly when confronted with challenging scenarios involving motion, blur, and low illumination. An accompanying study examines how well human observers can distinguish single pixels and provides a metric for evaluating anomaly detectability. This research is currently the basis of a participating task in the IVS-Anomaly Detection Challenge 2022. Additionally, ReD has emerged as the top-performing method in the competition, surpassing other techniques in anomaly localization accuracy while also exhibiting enhanced computational efficiency. A comparative evaluation of ReD's detection methods against competing approaches is also documented. Notably, an open-source variant of ReD, specifically designed for self-supervised training, demonstrates comparable results to its supervised counterpart in multiple anomaly detection tasks. We examine the structure of the pion using various form factor models, including the (PCAC) relation, Buchalla et al. formula, and a lattice QCD-based model. Our calculation of the pion vector form factor suggests a nonzero value at $q^2 = 0$, which contradicts the (PCAC) relation. The Buchalla et al. formula appears to be a reasonable approximation at low energy levels, but it doesn't fully account for the asymptotic high-energy behavior, which could be influenced by pion exchange. The shape factor for the pion vector form factor, when applied to the muon $(g-2)$ analysis, reduces the discrepancy between experimental and theoretical results by approximately $0.1\sigma$ for different coupled channels, which may improve with inclusion of additional pion processes. However, the total contribution from various pion processes to the muon $(g-2)$ analysis remains limited due to the relatively small effect of each process. Additionally, the direct calculation of the pion vector form factor in various models, including the vector-meson dominance model and a Dieterich et et al. model, confirms the existence of a nonzero value at $q^2 = 0$, which contradicts the (PCAC) relation. Our study also demonstrates that the shape factor for the pion vector form factor, depending on the chosen model, can be both positive and negative in the high-energy asymptotic range. Finally, when applying various pion form factor models to the muon $(g-2)$ analysis, the shape factor contributes a negative value to the result, which ranges approximately from $-0.3\sigma$ to $-0.6\sigma$. Such a contribution needs to be accounted for in further theoretical and experimental muon $(g-2)$ analyses to ensure accuracy. Based on our calculations involving different pion form factor models, we recommend performing a direct calculation using quantum electrodynamics and quantum chromodynamics to determine the pion vector form factor with necessary precision. The calculation should incorporate a proper description of the pion exchange interaction to avoid conflicts with the (PCAC) relation and various unitarity conditions. Furthermore, the direct calculation should be capable of providing quantitative information about pion-pion amplitude, which could be utilized in future studies on the pion resonance spectrum. In risk-aware reinforcement learning with safety constraints, limiting the risk of taking dangerous actions is crucial. The notion of dynamic regret is introduced to analyze adaptative reinforcement learning algorithms in risk-aware RL settings. Dynamic regret measures the discounted cumulative happiness within safety boundaries over a sequence of time steps that can be divided into phases, with each phase being a fixed number of steps called the horizon. Unlike stationary environments, where minimizing dynamic regret is simple, in non-stationary environments, where the reward and safety constraints frequently change, finding an optimal strategy is more complex. A new set of linear programming algorithms is developed to achieve near-optimal dynamic regret, with sublinear cumulative happiness within safety boundaries, in non-stationary environments with changing risk and safety constraints. These algorithms require knowledge of when the environment's parameters have changed, but without this information, a detection method is introduced to identify the environment's parameters, which also requires only a small number of samples. Finally, a new separation design is developed, with the ability to adaptively adjust its parameters,, which, allows it to achieve near-optimal dynamic regret, with sublinear cumulative happiness within safety boundaries, in non-stationary environments with changing risk and safety constraints. A series of numerical experiments, including one where an automaton operates in a uncertain 2D space, searching for a specific object while avoiding dangerous areas, demonstrate the performance of the developed algorithms, which need only a short time to adapt to changes in the reward and safety constraints. Our investigation centers on the enhanced PriReg procedure, a Bayesian approach for selecting regression model dimensions, particularly suited for situations with limited to moderate amounts of data and varying error variances unknown a priori. We examine PriReg's performance when dealing with a large number of potential variables, analyzing both general and specific settings. For the broader context, PriReg's effectiveness is assessed through an extensive simulation study, focusing on crucial aspects such as estimation bias and root mean square error. For the more confined scenario, where structural relationships underpin data generation, we establish precise, high-dimensional rate limits for PriReg's estimation accuracy. Notably, these limits remain applicable even in cases of strong correlations among variables. A comparative study against other dimension-selection methods reveals PriReg to be a robust and reliable choice across diverse problem scenarios. All theoretical findings are substantiated through numerical experiments, revealing PriReg to yield superior results, often surpassing Bayesian information criterion and consistency-based methods in various data settings. The analysis demonstrates that utilizing Bayes' Theorem to estimate uncertain parameters enhances the effectiveness of GA optimization. Additionally, the study highlights that optimizing machining centers using GA yields improved results when compared to the conventional technique of using a baseline design without optimizations. The key advantages of this research are the integration of uncertainty into the evaluation process and the use of GA optimization, which together enable the development of more energy-efficient and optimal machining center designs. This issue is examined in two scenarios, with and without an additional resonance, and in both cases, we develop an algorithm to eliminate the unwanted solution, yielding physically valid results. In the first scenario, the algorithm involves comparing effective and physical coupling values, while in the second, it involves integrating the amplitude using a specific condition, ultimately resulting in an integrated amplitude with correct physical properties. In both cases, we demonstrate the process with actual data. Additionally, we emphasize the importance of blending techniques in addressing issues with physical parameter extraction and potential pitfalls in amplitude fitting. Furthermore, integrating the amplitude in a specific manner also enables us to re-evaluate the decay constant associated with $\eta'$, which we do, and the resulting value aligns with standard scenarios involving heavy quarkonia and chiral symmetry breaking. In this process, we also derive an expression for the $\eta$-$\eta'$ mixing angle, which could be relevant in future, differentially analyzing, contributions from the anomaly. Lastly, we note that our integrated amplitude, despite incorporating the blending of $\eta$ and $\eta'$, does not include contributions from the anomaly, which may arise in specific scenarios, such as the process of radiation, and warrant further examination. In contrast to conventional wisdom, this approach predicts an approximately 40% value for the quadratic coefficient in the low-energy amplitude. The presence of a localized charge defect distorts the two-dimensional electron gas around it, resulting in spin-vortex states characterized by spin polarization. We demonstrate through analytical and numerical examinations that these spin-vortex states exhibit higher-order quantization. Specifically, we derive an effective Hamiltonian describing the electron system and employ a conformal field theory approach to determine the degeneracies of these spin-vortex states. The effective Hamiltonian features a set of spin polynomials, each associated with a specific Landau level, that generate the degenerate states through algebraic operations. We find that the spin-vortex states up to the seventh Landau level exhibit degeneracies consistent with type-I topological order, while higher-energy states show degeneracies inconsistent with the type-I topological order exhibited at lower energy levels. Additionally, we have developed a method to determine energy spectra of any spin-vortex state and have used this approach to calculate various degeneracies. Furthermore, we have developed a set of rules governing the algebraic relationships between spin-vortex states that explain their degenerate patterns, particularly in regards to the associated angular momentum, spin, and system density. The nature of the defect, either a charge density wave or a soliton, is shown to influence the energy spectrum through the Landau level-related factors and the spin polynomials. We have verified our analytical findings through numerical examinations of the effective Hamiltonian and the spin polynomials using a variational method, with our results revealing that these numerical approaches accurately predict the degeneracies and energy spectra around the localized charge defect. Lastly, we propose a wavefunction for a general spin-vortex state that encompasses the algebraic relationships between spin-vortex states and demonstrate that this wavefunction exhibits the same characteristics as the effective wavefunctions derived from the conformal field theory and the variational method. The degeneracy of the spin-vortex states is shown to increase with the energy level at a localized charge defect. The highest-energy state examined, corresponding to the seventh Landau level, exhibits a 1,672,553-fold degeneracy. Notably, the degeneracy of the spin-vortex states follows a specific pattern characterized by repeatedly applied sequences of algebraic operations, with our results suggesting an exponential increase in the degeneracy as a result of these repeated operations. We have identified multiple factors contributing to the degeneracy, including a primary contribution related to the associated angular momentum, a set of secondary contributions characterized by the spin polynomials corresponding to different Landau levels, and various higher-order contributions

Predicting the effects of online trends on society before they happen is known as social impact forecasting. Many methods have been proposed to address this issue, but most rely on extensive data sources and ignore the importance of predicting for an extended duration. This research tackles a social impact forecasting task by using graph neural networks to forecast the shift in online engagement when an influencer posts for a specified period. To train and test these models, we developed a new dataset through a crowdsourcing process that involves asking a group of people to predict changes in online metrics for various posts. This dataset is unique because it includes a range of forecast durations from a few hours to several days. To train our models, we combined training and testing data to increase the amount of information available. This approach is supported by experiments showing its effectiveness. When tested against methods relying on pre-trained models, our proposed method performed the best according to metrics such as mean absolute error and mean squared error. To validate our approach, we compared our predictions of shift in online engagement with actual data and found a positive correlation. This validation supports our decision to increase train and test durations to aid in model performance. A comparison with state-of-the-art methods was conducted and resulted in our approach being the most effective according to metrics such as mean absolute error and mean squared error. Specifically, we identify a pivotal inner product that governs the evolution of conformal block trajectories and ultimately yields the conformal field theory spectrum. Notably, this inner product exhibits a complex relationship, being a particular, 'folded' version of the inner product that governs the geometric fluctuations of metric perturbations. This intricate connection to geometric instability may contribute to the long-standing challenge of formally linking conformal field theory with Liouville conformal field theory. Lastly, our findings may also shed new light on the applications of Gromov's ideas to the broader realm of quantum physics. Additionally, our analysis underscores the beauty and universality of Euler-Arnold equations, which captivate through their multifaceted connections to geometric partial differential equations, symplectic geometry, and now, conformal field theory. Ultimately, this research may pave the way for novel approaches to studying conformal field theory and related fields, fostering a harmonious integration of pure mathematical insights with the recent breakthroughs and open problems in quantum physics. In particular, we hope this research may contribute to resolving the pivotal open problem of formulating a rigorous, $W$-algebra axiomatic framework for conformal field theory. In particular, our conclusions may hold promise for promoting the 'folded' inner product as a viable option for defining the central charge $c$ within this framework. Also, our analysis may inspire fresh insights into geometric stability and the second eigenvalue of the Laplacian, an area to which Gromov regrettably passed away before seeing the recent progress. We hope our findings may serve as a tribute to Gromov's profound legacy, promoting the eagle-like agility needed to grasp the intricacies of conformal field theory, as illustrated through the applications of Euler-Arnold equations. Lastly, these research notes may also represent a humble contribution to the broader project of 'geometry of quantum physics.' Furthermore, CLS can effectively handle the inherent uncertainties associated with signal propagation and environment-related factors, such as signal attenuation and multi-path interference, to provide reliable performance assessments. CLS can be applied in diverse scenarios involving multiple signal parameters and are demonstrated in this study through simulations and measurements focusing on target position and frequency. In cases where only noisy local rewards are available for learning policies, assuming the world model's objective as the master reward function becomes questionable. In situations where experts provide optimal action recommendations, but data is imperfect, learning a consistent policy from these suggestions becomes problematic. To address these issues, we present a new hierarchical Bayesian framework that separates role learning from policy learning. This framework enables us to effectively model unregulated tasks, align our approach with theoretical limitations, and develop robust policies using various inference methods, even with limited data. Additionally, we demonstrate the framework's capabilities by learning a policy in a partially observable, partially regulated environment with only weak supervision. Furthermore, we highlight the advantages of our framework over traditional end-to-end RL and mean-field approaches. Finally, we show that our framework can be adapted to tackle other reinforcement learning challenges, such as learning a master reward function. This adaptation surpasses previous methods and highlights the framework's potential for a wide range of real-world applications. Finally, we open-source our code for public use. In nontrivial cases, the transfer homomorphism for a finite group $G$ can be expressed as an algebraic combination of Abelian $p$-primary transfer homomorphisms for prime numbers $p$. Therefore, if we have a finite group $G$ and a $G$-module $P$, and the set of abelian $p$-primary transfer homomorphisms for $P$ is sufficiently distinct in the sense of having large enough ranks compared to the size of the $p$-Sylow subgroup of $G$, then this condition determines a corresponding region in the Bass-Serre tree space for $G$. This region, denoted as $\mathcal{B}_{P,\min}(S_G)$, represents the collection of all Bass-Serre trees for $G$ with reduced homology in $P$ that have ranks of their p-Sylow subgroups less than their orders. A similar but larger set, $\mathcal{B}_{P,\max}(S_G)$, consists of all Bass-Serre trees for $G$ with reduced homology in $P$ where the ranks of their p-Sylow subgroups do not exceed their orders. This work presents formulas for calculating upper and lower bounds on the rank of $\mathrm{tr}_{S_G}^{S_p}(P)$, the rank of the p-primary transfer homomorphism for $P$ and any prime number $p$ dividing $|G|$. These bounds imply that $\mathrm{tr}_{S_G}^{S_p}(P)$ is non-zero and strictly positive if and strictly greater than the size of the p-Sylow subgroup of $G$, and it follows that $\mathrm{tr}_{S_G}^{S_p}(P)$ is invertible if and only if $P$ is projective. This projectivity condition holds true even when checking individual subgroups of $G$ and further demonstrates the accuracy of the calculated bounds by verifying and extending a prior result which it also generalizes to a wider category of finite groups $G$. Notably, the method of verifying if a $G$-module is projective represents a new approach as it does not rely on group cohomology but rather on properties of small loops transfer regions. The initial creation of supermassive black holes remains an unresolved mystery in the field of astrophysics. As a continuation of our prior research, we present new findings from our comprehensive cosmological hydrodynamical simulations, specifically designed to model the origin of supermassive black holes. By repeating the simulation 20 times and employing a advanced agglomerate model, we've successfully predicted the mass distribution of supermassive black holes spanning a vast range, from a few millionths to a few billion times the mass of our sun. The predicted mass distribution matches closely with current observational data. A key outcome of our research indicates that supermassive black holes are most likely created when gas is drawn into dense galaxy cores at early cosmic epochs. The mass of these early created black holes is closely tied to the final mass of their host galaxies. Subsequent growth of these black holes is largely driven by the ongoing fueling of their surroundings with gas and star-formation. This fuel is eventually shut off when a mass-metrically chosen galaxy reaches a peak in its star-formation rate. This newly identified pattern of black hole and star growth challenges the long-held paradigm of a uniform, continuous growth of supermassive black holes. This research presents a promising scenario in which the seeds of supermassive black holes are planted at early cosmic epochs and then slowly grow into massive black holes over time. This newly discovered scenario could help to unify the diverse array of observed supermassive black holes seen today. This research may also aid in understanding the early creation of black holes with exceptionally large masses. The predicted mass distribution of supermassive black holes could be tested further using data from the upcoming James Webb Space Telescope. This research lays the foundation for future work, focusing on the global rate of supermassive black hole growth, as well as the role of (super)massive black holes in shaping their galactic environments. Their feedback affects the surrounding gas, ultimately controlling the creation of galaxies and their inherent (super)massive black holes. To effectively analyze the complex results of inelastic neutron scattering (IENS) experiments, it is crucial to first grasp the underlying quantum state of the material being studied, as these experiments are highly sensitive to its many-body interactions. However, interpreting IENS data is challenging due to its high dimensionality and ambiguity. Machine learning models can learn this complex interpretation, but they often lack transparency, making it difficult to trust their conclusions. This study presents a novel approach to tackling this issue by using a straightforward neural network design, consisting of a symmetric and layer-wise repeated series of linear transformations, to replicate the quantum state from IENS data, and demonstrates its application on a well-known model compound. This transparent neural network facilitates understanding the relationship between IENS data and the material's quantum state, and its calibration is easily replicated to analyze data from other experiments. Notably, this study showcases the first successful application of a neural network to calibrate IENS data, and highlights the promising prospects for neural networks in simplifying the interpretation of IENS data, thereby expanding the reach of neutron scattering research. In this paper, we introduce the concepts of a digital laboratory journal and a science ledger, aiming to capture the essence of laboratory activities through the documentation of experiments, associated observations, and outcomes. To make digital laboratory journalism accessible to a broad audience, we developed JavaScript-based tools that can be easily integrated into educational programs. We also outline the benefits of digital laboratory journalism, focusing on how it can facilitate the sharing of results, connect students with the wider scientific community, and promote open access to scientific data, ultimately accelerating the convergence of experimental findings towards a common goal. We demonstrate the functionality of these tools through a practical example of a digital laboratory journal tailored to the needs of chemistry or biochemistry students conducting UV-Vis spectroscopy. This protocol can be utilized as a standalone digital laboratory journal or integrated into the LMS platforms Moodle and OpenEdX for seamless distribution and shared execution. Furthermore, the associated code has been contributed to the GitHub repository for the benefit of the scientific community. We believe digital laboratory journalism holds immense potential to nurture responsible research practices and contribute to the collective advancement of scientific pursuits. As open digital laboratory journals, our approach and associated code can serve as versatile templates for promoting open access and fostering collaboration within various scientific communities. Due to their complex atomic arrangements, these materials have seen significant improvements in their mechanical and corrosion resistance properties. Nonetheless, understanding their structure at the atomic level and how it affects their overall composition remains an enduring mystery. To bridge this knowledge gap, computational tools have become indispensable, and machine learning algorithms in particular have made vital contributions in predicting the behavior and properties of these alloys. This editorial survey examines the progress made so far in using machine learning for HEA research and highlights promising avenues for further investigation. It is anticipated that this research will lead to the development of novel high-entropy materials with tailored properties. Nonetheless, to propel HEA research forward, there's a need for a standardized protocol in collecting and sharing data, as well as the development of user-friendly platforms for data storage and machine learning-based prediction. These initiatives will facilitate greater collaboration among the diverse groups working on HEA. Additionally, there's an pressing need for the implementation of machine-learned models in an experimental setting to validate their accuracy and usefulness. By tackling these challenges, machine learning can successfully bridge the gaps between atomic-scale data, macro-scale properties, and engineering applications of these materials. In this editorial, key issues and opportunities will be discussed, and their implications for the future of high-entropy alloys research aided by machine learning will be explored. It is expected that this research will lead to breakthroughs not only in materials science, but also in other data-driven fields. Moreover, the knowledge gained from this data-driven journey will create new avenues for educational and research endeavors. The $T_{cc}^+$, initially reported by LHCb in 2019, is a exotic hadron composed of three quarks in a specific arrangement. The study has examined how the $T_{cc}^+$, with a quark constitution of $c c \to c u$, decays into $D^{\ast} D \pi$ in distinct configurations and determined the respective partial decay widths. The research on Sidon sets has been intensively conducted by mathematicians. A subset is considered Sidon if its elements can be expressed as the sum of at most r distinct non-negative integers where r is the smallest possible number for that subset. We are able to demonstrate that if a subset with r=2 is added to a finite abelian group, the resulting combination will have a high degree of nonlinearity in line with current best-case scenarios as per Carmichael and Chatteraji's work. Additionally, various examples and theoretical proofs concerning Sidon sets and their exponents have been derived. We show that if a subset with r=2 is used for vectorial Boolean mappings, the resulting mappings will have a high degree of nonlinearity in line with current nonlinearity limits set by Karabasic and Prendiville. Furthermore, several narrow-sided Sidon sets with specific properties have been developed along with counting inequalities for Sidon sets with exponents. These have been theoretically and computationally validated. As a result, the nonlinearity of vectorial Boolean mappings has reached its highest possible extent (n-1)/2 in dimensions of n that are a product of two distinct primes and up to n/2 in all other dimensions. We have also developed narrow-sided Sidon sets with unique properties, including being closed under specific operations and its elements being evenly distributed in specific arrangements. The examples provided have been verified using number theory tools such as the prime number theorem and simon's work on cyclic groups. We have made connections between Sidon sets and other number theoretic concepts like quadratic forms and homology, presenting various generalizations and alternative expressions for Sidon sets. Furthermore, we have explored the transversality of Sidon sets and its consequences. We have also derived a method for generating Sidon sets using random numbers and established a method for determining the possible values within Sidon sets. We have made connections between Sidon sets and finite fields, presenting instances of Sidon sets in finite fields along with their cardinalities. We have also established a method for determining whether a subset can be Sidon or not based on its elements. We have made connections between Sidon sets and prime numbers, presenting instances of Sidon sets consisting only of prime numbers along with their exponents. We have also established a method for determining whether a number can be the sum of two integers or not based on its properties. We have made connections between Sidon sets and finite semigroups, presenting instances of Sidon sets in finite semigroups

In various real-world applications such as data classification, the large-scale training data is often presented in a binary matrix format. To achieve high training efficiency, a predefined margin is used with approximation techniques employed to speed up processing. A specific strategy involves randomly sampling the matrix to reduce processing time. However, the quality of trained models heavily depends on data quality. While reducing data volume through sampling can improve training speed, it also decreases model accuracy if the sampled data is not representative of the overall data set. To resolve this issue, a new algorithm is proposed to evenly sample binary training data based on class margins. Instead of randomly sampling entries or rows, this algorithm places rows into the dataset based on a calculated index which takes into account the fraction of each class it has encountered so far. A parameter called the sampling fraction determines the proportion of the initial data volume to use for training. Tests using the MNIST dataset for model initialization demonstrate that the proposed algorithm consistently outperforms uniform sampling methods. Additionally, comparing it to a strategy involving the incorporation of erosive functions to smooth model margins reveals it yields equivalent results with reduced processing time. Importantly, processing can be halted at any time and the model will still be usable with its margin intact. To confirm the general applicability of this algorithm, it was also successfully used for model retraining on the CIFAR10 dataset. A theoretical explanation for its effectiveness is provided, along with its source code available at https://github.com/graydog9/binary_sampling. To confirm the accuracy of the proposed algorithm, a validation set was used to compare its performance to the uniform sampling method. While it doesn't excel under the pre-defined metrics established by prior research, the proposed algorithm does consistently outperform it. A key finding is that the uniform sampling method actually performs better when the sampling fraction is low (i.e., less data is used for training) but deteriorates as the fraction approaches 1 (i.e., we're looking at nearly the entire data volume). In contrast, the proposed algorithm offers consistent performance across a range of sampling fractions. Furthermore, examining the impact of the algorithm on model regularization using a parameter called the margin fraction reveals its effectiveness in preserving model smoothness, features that are not readily quantifiable from the provided results but are evident in the provided figures. To conclude, the proposed algorithm offers consistent performance, reduced processing time, and a theoretical foundation for its suitability in binary matrix data training tasks. In this release, we introduce a modular approach to packaging these capabilities into reusable Java libraries, dubbed "modules," totaling 51 in number, along with a central tool for managing these modules, the ELKI Administration Tool (EAT). Additionally, we introduce a new framework for clustering algorithm evaluation, encompassing 34 indexing methods, 24 dimensionality reduction techniques, and 122 statistical measures. By initiating growth from a carefully selected idler frequency, parametric sowing limits fluctuations in the optical frequency spacing, thereby improving the coherence of the comb and its ability to support multiplexed communication systems. Numerical simulations model various microresonator configurations to demonstrate the effectiveness of parametric sowing in specific setups. Notably, by applying parametric sowing to a silicon microresonator with a high intrinsic Kerr nonlinearity, the researchers were able to achieve over 1 GHz of stable optical frequency spacing, paving the way for advanced applications in physics and engineering. Additionally, parametric sowing has been successfully demonstrated in a potassium titanyl phosphite microresonator with a photosensitive Kerr nonlinearity. The findings of this research offer promising avenues for integrating microphotonic parametric sowing systems into existing integrated optical circuits. Quantization has gained significant interest due to its capacity to reduce storage and processing requirements during inference. There's an underlying assumption that quantization also improves model generalizability, however this theory hasn't been thoroughly explored. This study delves into the quantization process and its effects on the neural network's behavior by analyzing the neural network's kernel, particularly within binary-weight-based architectures. Our investigation demonstrates that quantization strengthens the regularization effect within these networks, resulting in improved generalizability. This effect is shown to be amplified when using training methods that promote diversity among binary representations. Our findings are supported by experiments conducted on MNIST, CIFAR-10, and ImageNet datasets. Additionally, our analysis provides a practical approach to evaluating the generalizability of quantized models before implementing them on hardware. This analysis is exemplified by achieving comparable results on CIFAR-10 when applying the generalization boost effect to a pre-trained ResNet-18 model. Lastly, our study reveals the potential for improved practices in hardware quantization, suggesting that latency reductions shouldn't come at the cost of generalizability when the effect is optimized. The relationship between imaginary Gaussian free field (IGFF) and Schramm-Loewner evolution (SLE) is well documented, with the coupling of IGFF to SLE accounting for the stochastic spatial displacement of the stochastic process. Building on this foundation, this article explores new couplings of IGFF to multiple SLE systems, including those driven by random log-gases, random matrices, and random percolation. We establish that these new couplings are equivalent to conformal field theories with central charge less than zero, thereby providing a geometric interpretation of these models. We also derive new proofs of established facts, including conformal bootstrap and power law decay in sub-critical percolation, using the basis of IGFF-SLE-decorated structures. Lastly, this article concludes with an examination of the probabilistic theory of conformal field theory, highlighting distinct regimes and potential connections to the rational and trivial models. We also propose a new formula for the probability distribution of the Lévy process associated with an IGFF based on its stopping times linked to the SLE tractations. Verifying the outcomes of quantum computations is crucial, and the growing complexity of these algorithms makes traditional verification methods impractical. We've developed a new approach based on verifiable secret sharing that requires only a linear number of computations, regardless of the algorithm's complexity. Unlike existing methods, this one enables efficient verification for high-complexity quantum algorithms without compromising their performance. We've tested this approach with a scalable quantum approximation algorithm known as QAOA and found it to be significantly faster than traditional verification methods, though less accurate. Our solution includes a quantum-inspired sampling algorithm that's 2.3 times quicker than a comparable quantum simulation, according to available evidence. We've validated this improvement using high-performance computing, specifically 128 A100 GPUs. This work addresses a previously underappreciated challenge in quantum computing, namely how to efficiently verify complex algorithms. We've achieved this efficiency by allowing inaccuracies in exchange for faster processing times, effectively trading precision for throughput. This compromise is inherent to high-performance computing, particularly when many processes need to be parallelized, as is the case with our 128 GPU computations. Our solution includes a public-key encryption scheme designed for efficient encryption and decryption of binary data, including computational results. We've also devised a method for efficient generation and sharing of quantum states, effectively extending the traditional secret sharing technique to support quantum applications. This extension enables smooth integration of quantum algorithms into the existing secret sharing framework while enabling new quantum-inspired applications. Finally, we've introduced a new concept for measuring computational complexity, which serves as an objective indicator of how demanding an algorithm is to compute, regardless of the underlying technology used. This objective assessment facilitates a performance comparison of different algorithms, as demonstrated by our evaluation of how well the QAOA and its classical counterparts handle combinatorial optimization problems. This comparison included 11 datasets across three scenarios and showed that while the QAOA outperformed classical approaches on specific quantum-inspired sampling algorithms, it demanded significantly more computational resources, particularly when compared to faster, though less accurate, classical alternatives. Overall, our solutions involve an efficient quantum-inspired sampling algorithm; improved cryptographic schemes compatible with quantum computing; and a new approach to verifying quantum calculations based on verifiable secret sharing, all of which enable new combinations of quantum and classical techniques. Living cell structures exhibit intricate patterns requiring accurate and efficient
mathematical representations to facilitate computer simulation and analysis. Due to
the challenging nature of capturing these patterns, current methods relying on
level-set methods or surface mesh representations fall short, being either too
expensive or limited in their ability to represent complex dynamics. To address
these issues, we propose using implicit neural radiance fields (NeRFs) to model cell
shapes and patterns, leveraging their ability to efficiently represent complex
geometries and extend easily to three and four dimensions. Applying this method
to early embryo development in Xenopus laevis, we demonstrate the capability to
generate plausible 3D cell shapes and perform virtual experiments using the trained
models, resulting in actionable insights that could be exploited in future studies. 
Our approach does not necessitate domain expertise and can be easily adapted to other
cell types, making it a versatile tool for studying cellular behavior and patterns
in biology. The code for our model is available on GitHub at https://github.com/rotters/nerfcells.

The spectrogram is widely employed as a visualization tool, offering a comprehensive view of a signal's frequency domain content. While its common use implies a one-to-one correspondence between spectrogram levels and signal magnitude, this paper examines the geometric implications of extracting a signal's essential features from its spectrogram. These features are characterized by the signal's maximum and minimum values in the frequency-time domain. Specifically, this paper derives a statistical description of these features' distribution and develops an analytical method for estimating the spectrogram level contours that encompass a specified percentage of a signal's energy. This energy-based approach enables a comparison with traditional spectrogram level extraction methods, including popular ones like the parabolic and linear techniques. Furthermore, the introduced methods are demonstrated in a context of target detection and extraction from a noisy background. Notably, the introduced methods successfully detect targets with low signal-to-noise ratios (SNRs) below 4 dB, whereas the spectrogram level extraction methods achieve success rates for SNRs above 10 dB. We developed a new method to detect multiple synchronized groups and traveling chimeras in spiking neural networks using an extended phase-space strategy. This method is adaptable to networks of different sizes and topologies, as well as those with nonuniform connections. Without making assumptions about the specific form of the network's connectivity, it accurately identifies synchronized states and traveling waves. Furthermore, we demonstrated its ability to detect global chimera states in ring networks and group synchronization in tree structures. The proposed method also has the potential to be extended to more complex tasks, such as identifying dynamic transitions between different network states. Overall, this study showcases the effectiveness of the method and our numerical results indicate its robustness against perturbations. The associated code has been made publicly available for other researchers to access. Additionally, we explored the impact of different parameters on the stability and existence of chimera states, which may be useful for parameter regularization in low-dimensional systems. Our research extends the applicability of the phase-space method to larger and more diverse network configurations. Ultimately, this study lays the groundwork for future investigations into the general causes and consequences of chimera states in spiking neural networks. Random acceleration models are often employed as an alternative to more conventional gravitational potentials in studying N-body systems. Researchers use these models to explore the interplay between chaos and stochasticity and their respective influences on the dynamics of N-body systems. To contribute to such research, an implementation of a simple, uniform random force model has been added to the REBOUND N-body simulation code. This enhancement enables researchers to run N-body simulations using random acceleration models within the REBOUND framework. Building on prior work by Montb\^el\^on and Crouzeix, this implementation introduces a new method for conducting random acceleration simulations, which can serve as a force model in place of more conventional gravitational potentials. A particular case studied in this work involves the evolution of N-body systems under a time-stationary random force model with zero mean and a finite correlation time. Specifically, this research examines the differences in final system configurations resulting from two initial conditions: ordered and chaotic. These findings demonstrate that, under the random force model, subsequent evolution is largely unaffected by the initial condition, a notable outcome given the optimistic prediction made by Lyapunov in 1996. This work further extends REBOUND's capabilities, enabling researchers to utilize the code for studying N-body systems utilizing random acceleration models. A primary application of this new feature involves investigating the N-body system's dynamics resulting from the scattering of two groups of objects with varying densities and number of members, an area of study that was just beginning to emerge in the relevant literature at the time this work was conducted. This implementation offers a new tool for researchers working on N-body systems, specifically those utilizing random acceleration models, as they can now leverage the REBOUND framework to develop and validate their theoretical models. This new feature significantly expands the range of applications that can be explored within the REBOUND framework, ultimately contributing to a deeper understanding of the underlying dynamics of N-body systems. In this study, we explore how massive galaxies acquire supermassive black holes through accretion via star-forming processes or by merging with other galaxies. We simulate early universe events using a high-resolution computer model, recreating the formation of a galaxy similar to Leo I, which results in a supermassive black hole. Our goal is to identify observable indicators of each mechanism by comparing the predicted emission spectra from our model. Alternatively, we ask whether Leo I's peculiar MBH [inconsistent with typical relations] could serve as an indicator of its ancestral pathway. Using a specialized computer code, we model the galaxy's growth and the development of its supermassive black hole over 3 billion years. We consider two pathways: in one, the galaxy grows through star-forming events (smooth growth), and in the other, the galaxy grows through star-forming events but with periodic (10-200 million year) interruptions during which massive gas reservoirs are absorbed by a nearby, larger supermassive black hole (dynamical growth). Our smooth growth simulation yields emission spectra consistent with current MBH-galaxy relations, whereas our dynamical growth simulations produce anomalies in the MBH-galaxy relations predictable from their formation rates. Moreover, our dynamical growth simulations predict spectral emission signatures at low wavelengths (similar to radio wavelengths) related to the growth of the MBH and star-forming events, which are unobservable from our model of Leo I. Interestingly, our smooth growth simulations provide a plausible explanation for Leo I's MBH. For online advertising, accurately predicting click-through rates (CTRs) from push notifications is crucial for businesses to gauge the effectiveness of their content. However, push notifications often appear on mobile devices with impaired vision due to factors like low resolution displays, as their operators may not enable the enhancement for accessibility purposes. As a result, advertisers are typically provided with simplified text-based summaries of their content, which insufficiently represent the value of their visual elements. Given that visuals play a significant role in advertising, not being able to consider them hampers the forecasting of CTRs. To overcome this limitation, we have developed an end-to-end system called Vision-Based CTR prediction, capable of processing both text and visual components of advertisements. By combining the outputs from both a text-based model and a vision-based model, which analyzes both the textual and visual contents of advertisements, our system fills the information gap left by the standard push notification CTR forecasting methods. Through an examination of over 1 million real-world ads, we clearly demonstrate the advantages of our approach, as its integration substantially outperforms CTR forecasting alone, indicating a 26% improvement in accuracy. Additionally, our system is adaptable to datasets with various visual representation formats, including full-resolution images, thumbnail extracts, and screen captures, making it highly versatile and practical for use in real-world applications. Therefore, this research aims to address the critical issue of how to effectively incorporate visual elements into the forecasting of CTRs for push notifications, thereby enhancing the accuracy of advertisement performance prediction. As a result, this research can be utilized by businesses to further optimize the visual aspects of their content and maximize its potential when publishing new ads. The research provides evidence that incorporating visual elements significantly contributes to the prediction of advertisement performance, indicating a 26% improvement. Furthermore, the study highlights the feasibility of leveraging visual elements to predict the effectiveness of future advertisements. Case tools analyze these process models to identify issues and provide insights into problems and potential solutions. However, these case tools often fail to consider the scope of their recommendations. Traditional approaches to process reengineering classify changes as improvement or reengineering. Enterprise Resource Planning systems, used to automate processes, may struggle with irregular processes restricted by technical limitations. This research focuses on business processes constrained by technical limitations, specifically transactional systems, and is positioned within the reengineering paradigm. Wildfires disrupting global atmospheric systems pose significant financial losses, with resulting aerosols impacting climate change and human health. Forecasting aerosol levels accurately is crucial, yet tracking wildfire-induced aerosols is hindered by spatiotemporal aerosol variability and sparse ground monitoring stations. We propose an innovative approach, combining geostationary satellite data and physics-informed deep learning, to predict aerosol levels dynamically. Our method utilizes satellite data streams and numerical aerosol transport models to train a predictive model, which outperforms traditional forecasting methods, particularly in hard-to-predict regions. This deep learning framework can flexibly integrate various satellite data and transport models, enabling seamless aerosol transport modeling. We illustrate the system's effectiveness in a test case, predicting aerosol levels in California's 2020 wildfires. Our method has potential to guide wildfire risk assessment and aerosol forecasting globally. The code for this research is available at https://github.com/sohailrafiq/pinual.

The underlying architecture of 5G technology relies heavily on network functions virtualization (NFV) and software defined networking (SDN), which ultimately leads to the generation of large volumes of metadata. As a result, there is a pressing need to investigate the potential risks to privacy that can arise from this data and develop effective mitigation strategies. Specifically, our research aims to examine how an adversary can utilize metadata collected during the location tracking process to determine an individual's identity. We begin by analyzing different scenarios in which an adversary's prior knowledge varies, leading to the development of a framework that quantifies an individual's privacy based on entropy metrics. Furthermore, we investigate how varying parameters such as location updating frequency and system parameters impact an individual's privacy. Ultimately, we provide a comprehensive evaluation of our framework and study the interplay between privacy and efficiency under a practical use case. Interestingly, our results show that an adversary's prior knowledge significantly influences the disclosure of an individual's identity, while location updating frequency has a more substantial impact on privacy compared to system parameters. Additionally, our research reveals that an individual's privacy can be accurately estimated using our developed framework and that specific parameter values yield comparable privacy outcomes. Lastly, our research reveals that an adversary's privacy infringement can be condensed into a straightforward formula under a specific conditional prior distribution. Based on these findings, our research proposes a novel metric for evaluating an individual's privacy and proposes potential solutions to mitigate privacy breaches. Importantly, our research indicates that an individual's identification can be avoided if the adversary's prior distribution remains uncertain, the frequency of location updates exceeds a certain threshold, or a specific ratio of updates to measurements exceeds a certain value, which can be effectively utilized by service providers to strike a balance between an individual's privacy and the need for metadata. Current research using artificial intelligence to model brain connections often faces two significant issues: (1) biased data sets and (2) the limited understanding of prediction uncertainties. To tackle these problems, researchers tested a combination of preprocessing techniques aimed at enhancing cross-study prediction precision by reducing bias and improving uncertainty estimation. Specifically, they applied correlation-based data normalization and gradient feature scaling to resting-state fMRI connectivity data from a study involving 101 individuals, both with and without clinical symptoms of schizophrenia. By employing these preprocessing methods, we successfully demonstrated improved cross-study prediction precision, equivalent to a correlation of 0.90, at the group level. Notably, we also revealed significant individual differences in predicted connectivity patterns, which could potentially be utilized as individualized predictors. Lastly, we developed a method to estimate the reliability of predicted symptoms and other neurophysiological measures by attributing uncertainties to different stages of data analysis. Visual relocalization, a technique that retrieves a robot's location within a pre-built environment map, is crucial for autonomous mapping. While surfel maps offer efficient structure representation, they are often insufficient for visual relocalization due to sparse data points. Combining this approach with learned features from a neural network, we've developed a novel, fully automated relocalization system that leverages geometric constraints along with learned features to accurately determine a robot's location. The performance of our method was tested using a dataset comprising 16 sequences, and we achieved a 0.65 meters median error with as few as three geometric constraints. The results outperform previous surfel-based approaches and demonstrate superior performance with additional geometric constraints. Moreover, our method exhibits reliable performance across diverse environments with as few as two geometric constraints. The code for this approach can be found at https://github.com/Innovation-Orbit/surfel-map-relocalization. Federated learning is a decentralized machine learning technique that processes data across multiple devices without exchanging data itself. However, it struggles with developing models in the early stages of training and when dealing with semi-supervised data, particularly if there's no clear class structure. We've identified a issue where the model's weight distribution becomes ambiguous and noisy, mainly due to the data's label ambiguity and network communication issues. We've also found a way to mitigate this problem by using a simplified model structure. Specifically, we've trained a linear model on aggregated data and calculated its weight distribution, effectively reducing ambiguity. The proposed method has shown promising results, especially for semi-supervised data, and outperforms other techniques by a considerable margin. For instance, it has improved semi-supervised image classification by 92.55% and sentence classification by 84.44% compared to other models. We've opened-source this method to allow for its use in real-world applications. We've also explored its potential to adapt to different data distributions and found that it effectively handles a variety of datasets, largely due to its computational efficiency and data-independent factors. We've demonstrated its effectiveness on a range of datasets, primarily because it's influenced more by data-dependent factors and less by computational ones. The details of this method are located at https://github.com/dzhyde/Ambiguity-Reduction-for-Federated-L Learning. It has the potential to be an excellent foundation for future decentralized machine learning development. We've also identified several possible enhancements for future research. Firstly, we can utilize more advanced model structures, such as ResNet. Secondly, we can establish a data-dependent confidence metric to streamline network communication. Lastly, we can employ the federated augmentation technique to further decentralize the training process. We intend to investigate these possibilities further. It is noteworthy that the particular techniques we suggested for future research are not essential to the current method but do represent viable options for future development. Lastly, we believe that our work successfully establishes a solid theoretical base for decentralized semi-supervised learning and opens up new avenues for the community to explore. It has been successfully tested and shown to yield positive results. We've also provided a detailed breakdown of the model's performance, exceeding our initial expectations, and provided insight into its future potential research directions. In emergency medicine, priority setting is often a complex issue. Beyond immediate life threats, decisions about intervention duration can significantly impact patient wait times. Research has yielded generic guidelines on processing emergencies; however, these guidelines lack consideration for variation in intervention lengths. As a result, patients with shorter issues wait longer than those with longer issues, despite both requiring attention. To address this, we examined wait times as a function of intervention duration, collecting real-world data from the Bronx Municipal Hospital. Using a statistical model, we analyzed this data and derived a distribution of wait times for any given procedure duration. Furthermore, we identified specific procedures with unusually long wait times and applied this approach to an ideal-scenario hospital setting, demonstrating its potential for optimizing emergency room operations. By quantifying the impact of intervention duration on wait times, this analysis provides a foundation for decision-making in emergency medicine settings. Ultimately, this foundation can be used for deciding interventions that balance overall healthcare productivity and fairness. Through data-driven approaches, such as the one presented, we can generate practical, real-world solutions for complex decision-making processes. Research investigated the phenomenon of chiral magnetic effects within heavy ion collisions, specifically examining the interactions between charges and azimuthal distributions of particles in relativistic heavy ions. Analysis was based on data from the ALICE experiment, which took place at the CERN LHC for collisions with lead ions at 2.76 and 5.02 TeV. Indications of CME influence were sought via specific signal-to-background ratios in charged particle interactions. To minimize potential biases related to electric charges, researchers utilized complete hadron pairs composed of electrons, muons, and photons. This approach helped reduce effects of radial and elliptical flow influences on the data. However, contrary to predictions made by theoretical models, experimental data did not demonstrate CME influences as anticipated. Rather, differences in azimuthal angle distributions of charged particles only suggested their collective behavior was affected by radial and elliptical flow. These findings agreed with assessments of background influences, which also failed to demonstrate CME interactions. Thus, experimental data validated predictions made through perturbative QCD and saturation models. These findings underscored the need for novel interactions that can address limits of conventional particle physics models at LHC energies. Finally, these experiments underscored the importance and challenges of accurately measuring CME influences within heavy ion collisions at modern particle colliders.

The practice of crowd-supported funding has become more conventional, enabling anyone to secure funding by engaging audiences who, motivated by altruism or self-interest, contribute to achieve a shared goal. This research investigates the relationship between quantitative measures of crowd engagement and the success of campaigns on platforms like Kickstarter, Indiegogo, and Fundraising Champion, as well as events on DonorsChoose. Analyzing transaction data and campaign metadata from various platforms, our findings reveal which metrics predict a successful outcome. Additionally, we pinpoint the distinct characteristics of successful campaigns, highlighting differences between platforms in the roles that crowd interaction and campaign promotion play in achieving goals. This research aims to generate actionable insights for campaign organizers to enhance their chances of success by strategically manipulating crowd-facing elements, such as descriptions and updates, to attract the right audience at the right stage of their campaign. Utilizing a multi-method, cross-domain approach, this study expands our understanding of crowd dynamics across different platforms and the strategies needed to succeed in each environment. It also identifies opportunities for further research by linking existing literature to real-world campaign practices. Finally, this research contemplates new control mechanisms that could further the potential of crowd funding if effectively used, such as updating donors about the campaign's progress or showcasing donor recognition to retain existing supporters and win over new ones. Cybersecurity issues and related cyber losses are escalating at an alarming rate, largely due to the overwhelming number of cyber threats overwhelming the capacity of current defense systems, the difficulty for organizations to collect and share threat data due to data privacy concerns, and the lack of sophisticated techniques such as transfer learning to address novel threats. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel framework based on federated learning for sharing threat intelligence across different organizations. The framework utilizes Python's IMDB, IMDB-Movie Reviews, and WNSP datasets to build a Federated Learning based Network Intrusion Detection System. The results show significant improvements in classifying novel classes with test accuracy rates of 88%, as well as addressing the data privacy issue through shared representations with 93% accuracy. The novel approach offers a promising solution to the pressing need for enhancing the efficiency and scalability of current intrusion detection systems. The proposed framework consists of five layers and is outlined in two implementations: the Static FLIDS using pre-trained word2vec vectors and fine-tuned using static labels, and the Dynamic FLIDS where we employ word2vec vectors and labels from unbalanced datasets and update with balanced data using federated learning. The latter implementation outperforms the former with even distribution of data and test accuracy rates exceeding 90%. The code for this paper is available on GitHub at https://github.com/jbarral1/Federated-Learning-IDS. The outcome enables the extension to other applications beyond intrusion detection systems, such as detecting various types of attacks. Additionally, the research explores the feasibility of employing other techniques such as learning word embeddings with fastText, transferring learning with pre-trained models, and incorporating more sophisticated neural network architectures. The latter achieved an impressive test accuracy rate of 92% using pre-trained IMDB-Articles dataset. Furthermore, the research brings near a long-desired goal of learning a universal noise-robust representation for recognizing novel and novel-like threats. The task of developing a simulation environment for robotic manipulation sequences is a complex one, requiring rapid generation of valid sequences to support efficient robot simulation. In this context, we introduce an innovative, greedy approach to clustering tasks in order to enhance the performance of robotic manipulation sequence generation. Building upon existing sequence generators, our method employs clustering techniques to group tasks together based on their characteristics, effectively reducing the complexity of sequence generation. By applying this approach, we've achieved substantial time savings in generating robot manipulation sequences, averaging a 35% reduction in time. Our method does so without compromising the quality of the generated sequences, as assessed through metrics such as sequence length and diversity. Notably, the number of clusters can be adjusted to prioritize either the efficiency of sequence generation or the quality of the generated sequences, striking a balance between these competing factors. By incorporating our greedy clustering method, sequence generators can attain improved performance, demonstrated through experimental results using the Sawyer robot. A comprehensive online video showcases the clustering process and the generated sequences for a particular demonstration. The associated code for this research is openly available on GitHub at the provided link. Additionally, an online tool can be accessed at the specified URL to explore the clustering process and generated sequences, featuring interactive visualizations and embeddings of the sequence generator's memory module. Moreover, the Sawyer robot environment used in this research is openly accessible through the Robotic Arm simulator, allowing for reproducible results. Furthermore, a section has been included in the paper outlining potential generalizations of this research, including the application to other domains beyond robotic manipulation. The main contributions of this research can be summarized as follows. An innovative, greedy approach to clustering tasks is introduced, leveraging this clustering to enhance the performance of robotic manipulation sequence generators. The efficacy of this method is validated through experimental results, showcasing its capacity to attain superior performance by adjusting the number of clusters while generating high-quality sequences. The associated code, online tool, and open-source simulator have been made available for reproducibility purposes. Furthermore, a section has been included in the paper outlining further research generalizing these findings to other domains. The clustering method can be utilized as a standalone tool to optimize existing sequence generators, demonstrated through its effectiveness in enhancing the performance of the STR monte-carlo planner. The novel direction of this research was initiated by analyzing the performance of different sequence generators using a cluster-based approach, revealing distinct clustering patterns and validating the method's reliability through repeated evaluations. This study reports the development of highly versatile MOSFETs utilizing a standard 300mm CMOS process, combining both high-speed and low-voltage capabilities. By integrating a body tie and a light body tie, we engineered a novel MOSFET structure that facilitates high on-resistance without compromising the device's efficiency. Both numerical models and experimental results confirm the high performance of this design. Additionally, we have developed a corresponding circuit simulator, which accurately replicates the behavior of our highly agile MOSFETs within various circuit applications. Using this simulator, we analyzed the functionality of two transistors fabricated using different tie configurations, demonstrating their resilience to voltage fluctuations and high-temperature conditions. Moreover, we employed the simulator to design a highly versatile digital circuit, demonstrating an operating speed of 1GHz at 1V and 0.7V, respectively. All experiments were conducted using 300mm wafer test vehicles. Our research strives to make highly adaptable MOSFETs more accessible for various digital circuit applications. By integrating a body tie, we successfully manufactured high-speed and low-voltage transistors, showcasing an on-resistance variation of 0.5nm and performance resilience to 250°C and voltage fluctuations (±20%) beyond specifications. Furthermore, our test vehicles displayed an on-resistance variation as low as 0.5nm. We believe our findings will facilitate the widespread adoption of highly agile MOSFETs in diverse digital circuit designs. Moreover, we have observed a significant correlation between tie configuration and resistor distribution, which could guide future research efforts. Finally, our research suggests the vast potential of tie configuration variations in optimizing MOSFET performance, paving the way for future developments in this field. It is anticipated that these ties will play a crucial role in the development of beyond-logic-scale technologies. Our study could also inspire novel applications of tie configuration concepts, extending beyond digital circuit design to the fabrication of advanced semiconductor materials. One area we envision exploring in the future involves incorporating these ties in quantum structures, which could pave the way for the development of quantum devices using CMOS technology. Additionally, we plan to investigate the feasibility of incorporating quantum boxes tied together to enable the scalable manufacturing of high-performance quantum devices. It is also hoped that our research will yield novel mechanisms to regulate and enable the transition of these quantum devices, ultimately facilitating the development of efficient quantum processors using CMOS technology. The concept of team synchrony, defining the coordinated activity of multiple interconnected neurons within a neural network, has been studied extensively through the lens of spectral distance, identifying various threshold values and associated metrics that aid in quantifying synchrony across different natures of neural connections. To further explore team synchrony, this study examines how team synchrony scores change when individual neuron parameters are modified, revealing their independence despite their interconnection. Furthermore, as a generalization of previous work on team synchrony, this study also investigates synchrony among sub-teams of a larger group of neurons, revealing a correlation between the synchrony scores of these sub-teams and the overall group's cohesion. Ultimately, this study demonstrates the potential for intragroup neural connections to play a role in the formation of cohesive groups through their effects on neuron parameters.
