The diversity of origins in video search outcomes can influence how global events are perceived, thereby making it essential to verify the existence of diversity variety biasing (VVBS) - the difference in diversity of video origins retrieved for two search queries of varying nationality. To verify VVBS, we develop a novel approach using human-generated captions for domain-specific search queries and assess its practical application for evaluating global event coverage in video aggregates. Furthermore, we introduce the creation of fake agents to verify VVBS on a real-world video search platform, thereby confirming the presence of VVBS across various video platforms and domains, including sports, entertainment, and educational content. Our method enables the auditing of VVBS across numerous video platforms and domains, ultimately leading to the development of techniques to mitigate this bias and increase diversity in video aggregates. For example, our findings suggest that incorporating video captions from global contributors can significantly reduce VVBS, thereby enabling content curators to make more informed decisions when aggregating global videos and promoting a broader understanding of global events among viewers. The impact of our study can be observed in the increased exposure of global videos to a broader audience, ultimately shaping their perspective on global events. To facilitate reproduction of our findings, we publicly share our code and data on origin-bias, which can be applied to various video platforms and domains for evaluation of diversity variety biasing and potentially leading to the development of methods to mitigate this bias. Moreover, our study lays the groundwork for employing virtual agents in video aggregate auditing, thereby expanding the range of applications of this technique beyond diversity variety biasing. For instance, the approach could be utilized for detecting origin-based propaganda, verifying the presence of national perspective biasing (PVBS) - the difference in perspective of video origins retrieved for two search queries of varying nationality, or even identifying videos promoting hate speech. In summary, our method provides a pioneering approach to utilizing virtual agents for video aggregate auditing, thereby enabling content moderators to make informed decisions during video moderation and content review, ultimately leading to the development of content policies and algorithms to mitigate various biases in video aggregates, as demonstrated in our case study on diversity variety biasing. Additionally, our study reveals the potential applications of virtual agents in video aggregate auditing, extending beyond diversity variety biasing to detection of hate speech, origin-based propaganda, and national perspective biasing. Building upon the recent findings of [arXiv:2101.02764], where the relation between two-point functions and monodromy defects in the Wess-Zumino model was investigated, we delve deeper into the subject by examining the lattice regularizations and solving bootstrap equations for these regularized models. We find that the two-point function solutions obtained from lattice regularizations and monodromy defects share a strong resemblance, particularly in the ultra-violet (UV) limit. Notably, the key distinction lies in the behavior of the chiral primary operator's two-point function associated with the monodromy defect, as compared to its counterpart in the lattice-regularized model. We propose a conjectured extension of the renormalization group equation for the Wess-Zumino model, incorporating monodromy defects, and demonstrate the consistency of this conjecture with the monodromy defect's properties. We also explore the relationship between monodromy defects and lattice regularizations, positing that any valid lattice regularization, capable of capturing the model's physical behavior, should be equipped with a defect limit. We refer to this limit as a "self-consistent" defect, and illustrate its consistency with the bootstrapped monodromy defect through the example of the Wess-Zumino model in two dimensions. We anticipate that our work will serve as a foundational starting point for the analysis of other interacting monodromy defects, potentially within ket-theoretic frameworks as well. Additionally, we hope that our novel regularization technique will find applications across a broader theoretical physics landscape, encompassing regularized studies of quantum field theories. It is also feasible that monodromy defects may hold promise for conceptualizing novel quantum gravity phenomena, thereby contributing to the ongoing debate regarding the structure of quantum gravity as illustrated by the holographic principle. We hypothesize that monodromy defects could serve as a valuable tool for the exploration of quantum gravity, given their underlying connection to time evolution in the form of a non-linear operator as seen in examples of time-like defects. We anticipate that our work will facilitate fresh perspectives on these foundational issues in quantum gravity, further enabling the community to utilize the wisdom gleaned from the Wess-Zumino model to tackle these challenging queries in the realm of quantum gravity. It is plausible that leveraging monodromy defects will reveal novel, distributional solutions to the space-time structure of quantum gravity, thereby providing insight into the discrete nature of space-time at the sub-Planckian scale

We demonstrate the existence of elliptic curves, defined over cubic cyclic fields, present in 43 separate families, which possess 13 points of torsion. These curves are defined using a specific type of polynomial, known as trinomials, and as a result, possess certain distinct properties. To contribute to the Mordell-Weil conjecture and the rank distribution in elliptic curves, we provide a mathematical expression for the rank of these curves, based on previous work by Darmon, Rotger, and Vance, and further extend existing research by showing 13 is the maximum possible rank for these curves. Additionally, we provide a detailed explanation of how our curves satisfy the requirements outlined by Frey in 1992 for elliptic curves over number fields with specific rank and Galois action. These curves have cyclic cubic fields as their base and are known to be pairwise non-isomorphic, as well as demonstrating prime conductor. We have successfully verified the existence of these curves through computational verification using the software package Singular, in conjunction with the elliptic curve database Ecole. Furthermore, we have utilized ECHAP to investigate the arithmetic of these curves and accurately calculated key values of their function ring. These calculations have been confirmed via verification using Singular. We have compiled a comprehensive list of the 43 families mentioned above, along with additional information regarding the key values of their function ring, and made this available as reference material in conjunction with the full text of this article. We have elected to exclude the specific polynomials themselves from the public domain, in order to avoid providing support to malicious entities through access to these curves, as described by Frey in 1992. These curves can, however, be easily modified to eliminate their connection to Frey's problem, should their properties require such protection. We have also chosen to exclude the detailed analysis of how our curves satisfy certain distinctness criteria, due to the extensive computational verification required, but instead provided a simplified explanation in the initial sections of this article. We have also excluded a separate investigation concerning curves defined using quadratic polynomials, as this would have further expanded the public domain to include an extensive list of curves, and as such, we have instead provided a simplified overview and reference to existing research. These references, along with the full text of this article, include a comprehensive computational verification, utilizing the Singular software, along with echap, and listing the 43 curves, as well as a publicly available database. In dense wireless networks, similar signal strengths from multiple sources can cause interference, reducing overall network efficiency. This study focuses on high-density WiFi networks affected by interference from devices sharing the same channel, resulting in decreased network performance. To mitigate these effects, this work proposes a probabilistic approach to managing interference, ensuring a stable queue in WiFi routers. By modeling and analyzing the correlation between interference and packet transmission, this proposal utilizes a differentiable approximation to create a network model. Austenitization-based methods are applied to derive an expression for queue stability, confirming stability under specific conditions. Simulation results demonstrate the theoretical findings and show the potential for further improvements. The analysis and results provide insights for designing algorithms addressing correlated interference in wireless networks. An open-source code for this research is available at https://github.com/el-aziz/STIMC. Preliminary versions of this work were presented at IEEE ICC 2020 and IEEE WCNC 2021. Graph node classification is a fundamental problem that many studies have addressed. Despite notable advancements, current methods face challenges when dealing with large datasets due to their limited label availability. To tackle this issue, we propose an approach that combines unsupervised and supervised training to leverage abundant unlabeled data and minimize the requirement for labeled data. Building on pseudo-labeling techniques, we suggest generating high-confidence pseudo-labels for unsupervised nodes using an ensemble of trained models. These pseudo-labels are incorporated into the loss function with a weighting scheme that adjusts the balance based on the number of labeled and unsupervised nodes. To prevent overfitting, we employ noise to be introduced during the training process. Experimental results on standard benchmarks and real-world datasets showcase the effectiveness of our method, achieving comparable performance to state-of-the-art methods with significantly reduced labeled data. In video processing tasks, like super-resolution, we often encounter problems due to the long-range motion between frames, which can make traditional models with global assumptions ineffective. These models tend to overlook the local details present in nearby frames, limiting their performance. To overcome these challenges, we've developed PatchNet, a novel approach built on patch-based matching techniques, which takes advantage of short-range motion to efficiently align frames. By doing so, PatchNet can learn from the characteristics of small regions, ultimately resulting in improved resolution and detail in video processing tasks. Through experimentation, PatchNet has achieved impressive results, surpassing state-of-the-art methods in SR, ESR, and denoising tasks, while also training much faster. Notably, PatchNet can be extended to general motion scenarios, enabling end-to-end visual feature extraction from videos. These capabilities make PatchNet a versatile tool, well-suited for video processing tasks and beyond. To demonstrate the efficacy of PatchNet, we've conducted extensive experiments showing its superiority over existing approaches. These results, along with code and data, can be found on our repository: https://github.com/IMIMIDV/patchnet. A model of a multi-service wireless system, incorporating simultaneous wireless information and power transfer (SWIPT), is analyzed. It involves a multi-carrier transmission method utilizing Gaussian AM-PM combinations, which allow for efficient separation of received signals through a technique known as independent component analysis (ICA). These signals represent data and energy streams that may be corrupted by noise on various carriers. To resolve the issue of signal interference and noise, an optimization problem is developed, aiming to maximize energy availability while ensuring data rate requirements are met. This is achieved using a method that allocates power to currently active sub-carriers in a manner optimized for the specific application. As a result, a theoretical bound on energy availability with minimal data rate loss can be obtained. These findings are validated through comparisons with alternative systems, which demonstrate the efficacy of the proposed method. Consequently, this approach can streamline the design of SWIPT systems by eliminating the need for expensive and complex signal processing infrastructure. Ultimately, a standardized platform for designing SWIPT systems that strike an optimal balance between data transmission quality and energy efficiency can be established. It provides a comprehensive framework for designing efficient SWIPT systems that account for the specific requirements of various applications. This includes data transmission rate, energy harvesting needs, and service-specific constraints, which can be met through the careful selection of sub-carriers and corresponding power allocations. As a result, a general design approach for efficient SWIPT systems that can be applied to a range of applications with diverse energy harvesting and data transmission needs can be established. This involves using the derived theoretical bounds to develop simplified protocols for improving the overall efficiency of SWIPT systems. These protocols can be used to streamline the design of efficient SWIPT systems and provide a useful framework for designers and developers. It allows for the application of the principles of efficient SWIPT system design to a range of problems and ultimately enables the creation of improved SWIPT systems capable of providing a range of benefits through the careful selection of sub-carriers and corresponding power allocations. This polynomial is referred to as a universal Airy polynomial. Its coefficients are dependent on specific functions, $G_{3,N}(z)$ and $F_{3,N}(z)$, which are part of random matrix theory's matrix elements. These matrix elements play significant roles in understanding the local and semi-circle laws. This work extends the existing concepts in universal Airy polynomials presented in arXiv:2001.03467 to a broader domain. In interior point methods (IPMs), where an iterative procedure is employed to solve a linear equation system derived from a quadratic optimization problem with inequalities, specialized solvers for sparse matrices are often used. We investigate whether the termination condition "residual smaller than tolerance" in multigrid and preconditioned solvers adds additional computational expense in IPMs. Since these solvers commonly rely on multigrid methods, which may not provide a precise indication of convergence, an alternative "stagnation criterion" is explored as a potential inner loop termination condition. The preconditioned conjugate gradient solver, which is a multigrid component in CHOLMOD for example, typically requires about five iterations to reach its convergence threshold. As a consequence, an inner loop stagnation criterion may significantly reduce the overall computational cost of IPMs by avoiding premature outer loop iterations. The proposed inner loop stagnation criterion thus modifies the conventional IPM convergence test, potentially resulting in a longer path from an optimal interior solution to the optimal solution along with decreased overall computational costs. The proposed approach therefore introduces a dimensional change in the algorithm's time complexity without outside controls. The impact of inner loop stagnation is studied in detail through numerical experiments involving a variety of optimization problems with inequalities and dimensions up to 5000x5000. The modification leads to a notable reduction in overall computational costs for dimensional interior point methods, accurately utilizing the outer loop iterations provided by the algorithm. The code for replicating these results is made publicly accessible. Furthermore, two possible variations of inner loop stagnation, labeled 'inner-stagnation-1' and 'inner-stagnation-2', are defined. The first option identifies when an inner loop converges prematurely and refuses to advance the outer loop iteration as a result, whereas the second option delays outer loop progress only after two inner loop stagnations have occurred. The code for these variations is also made available on GitHub. The inner loop stagnation at present lacks a theoretically established limit but shows promise of lowering overall computational costs for dimensional interior point methods, accurately utilizing the outer loop iterations provided by the algorithm. The proposed inner loop stagnation at present does not satisfy the criteria for both fastest overall computational performance and optimal solution quality, though it does meet the criteria for both fastest overall computational performance and optimal solution quality under specific problem conditions. The code for replicating these results is made publicly accessible. However, widespread awareness of these limitations and necessary precautions often lacks, resulting in highly unlikely but potentially catastrophic consequences. Several instances have already materialized, including fatalities, accurate forecasts of grid ties that were not acted upon, and harm to relationships due to misinterpretation of audio. This paper proposes the establishment of the AI Incident Repository, allowing power users to share their experiences with failed or potentially hazardous AI implementations, including workarounds for future reference. By sharing documented incidents, we hope to raise awareness of potential failures, prompting discussions within the AI community about inherent risks and necessary safeguards to avoid severe repercussions in high-stakes applications. Three actual incident cases serve as motivation for this initiative, highlighting the need for a centralised repository that can facilitate the development of best practices and ensure that workarounds are incorporated into future AI systems. Two possible applications for the AI Incident Repository are explored, including its potential as a resource for providing recommendations on established AI services or as a companion to AI services as an alert system for potential hazards. This concept was presented during a NeurIPS 2021 workshop focused on promoting transparency and incident reporting within the neural network community. Since then, a publicly accessible AI Incident Repository has been made available, featuring over 180 documented incidents and continuing to expand with community contributions. For more information, the reader is referred to the repository, located at incident-reports.ai. Current business process management methods concentrate on visual representations of processes but overlook the inherent conflicts and ambiguities embedded in these processes. As a result, existing process analysis techniques cannot guarantee correct outcomes, leading to undesired consequences like premature process termination or incomplete data loss. To address these issues, we introduce a new process management approach called hybrid process specifications that integrate imperative and declarative elements to explicitly address the ambiguities and conflicts within the process. We also develop automated systems to evaluate hybrid process specifications' correctness and define operations to resolve the inherent contradictions. These automated systems can be applied as online supervisors during process execution to ensure consistency and provide the means to analyze and refine the process as well. We illustrate the efficacy of our approach through a real-world example originating from the healthcare sector. Finally, we identify potential future research avenues stemming from the complexities of hybrid process specifications. In complex graph-based modeling, a structured, precise representation of a function, particularly a multi-linear one, can lead to inefficient computation due to elevated memory requirements, making some optimization methods impractical. We have introduced a more efficient representation, the Brief Function, a compact summary of a multi-linear function that omits unnecessary variable interactions. This innovation enables exact Maximum Probability Explanation and efficient constrained optimization within graph-based models, while significantly reducing memory usage compared to traditional methods. We have analytically derived bounds on the memory savings in terms of model specifics. Experimental evaluations have demonstrated the scalability and efficacy of this approach, resulting in substantial memory savings without compromising accuracy, allowing previously unmanageable problems to be solved. This includes a linear model with 281 variables and another with 138 variables from computer vision, both of which could be solved exactly within 12 hours in a standard desktop. We have open-sourced this research, including source code and data, at https://github.com/alexih2/brief_functions. This research has been partially funded by ANR-18-CE48-0025 and Google Focused Award. It has led to a new company, Brief AI. Both can be found at brief.ai.

The viscosity shift towards higher shear rates in disordered suspensions undergoes a dramatic transformation from a non-Newtonian to a Newtonian behavior near a critical density, a phenomenon prevalent in shear thickening suspensions. A universal, global correlation exists between the critical density and the critical stress needed for this transition to occur in suspensions with varying particle shapes, allowing for a broader understanding of this phenomenon. Additionally, a theoretically derived scaling argument based on particle size and type confirms this observation, opening up possibilities for a more general application of this model and its potential to uncover underlying mechanics behind shear thickening. A simplified, effective medium model is proposed that explains the origin of a critical density and stress through volume fractions of particles and their increased resistance to deformation at high shear rates, leading to a softer and more dilute effective medium. This model not only predicts but also rationalizes numerous experimental findings in the literature. A simplified, strong-deformation limit of a previous model applied to granular materials also explains the observed global correlation without relying on specific particle contact mechanics, highlighting the widespread occurrence of shear thickening and its connection to soft and dilute particle assemblies. Radiation oncologists rely on computed tomography (CT) scans to create a customized treatment plan for patients with gastrointestinal cancers. Accurately defining the CT image volume that encompasses the gastrointestinal (GI) canal is crucial, as it enables healthcare professionals to assess the cancer's progression and administer targeted radiation therapy. Currently, defining the GI canal's boundaries is a time-consuming, labor-intensive process, typically requiring several hours of manual adjustment per image volume. In order to streamline this process, we've developed an automated deep learning algorithm capable of rapidly and accurately delineating the GI canal's boundaries within CT image volumes. Leveraging a diverse, high-quality training dataset consisting of 192 CT image volumes with annotated adjustments, our deep learning algorithm achieved notable improvements, specifically a sphere overlap score of 57.9% and a distance metric of 5.47 mm, as compared to the performance of human radiation oncologists. Furthermore, in tests conducted using CT image volumes depicting pathologies in the upper and lower GI tracts, our algorithm demonstrated robust generalizability, specifically a sphere overlap score of 43.9% and a distance metric of 7.01 mm. Notably, our algorithm consistently outperformed other unsupervised segmentation methods, as well as a supervised pre-trained model, in evaluating its effectiveness. Based on these results, our algorithm successfully trained and applied to diverse CT image volumes, demonstrating its ability to accurately and rapidly identify the GI canal's boundaries, ultimately streamlining the radiation therapy planning process. Additionally, we've made our algorithm and training data openly accessible, enabling healthcare professionals to further refine its capabilities by adjusting the algorithm and re-training it using their institution's local datasets. In doing so, our algorithm intends to ultimately enable healthcare professionals to quickly and easily customize radiation therapy plans for patients with gastrointestinal cancers. The exoplanet sample compiled by CORALIE and HARPS allows us to investigate how many planets with masses similar to Saturn's exist in close orbital paths. We examined over 1,300 planets with masses ranging from 0.1 to 10 times the mass of Earth and evaluated their orbital distances, finding that most (about 80%) of these planets with lower mass have counterparts within a specific ratio. Notably, our analysis found no instance of the "desert" - a term that describes a lack of planets with masses similar to Saturn's in close orbital paths. We attribute this phenomenon to several factors, including how planetary orbits are detected and how planets with mass and size comparable to Saturn are found. Pre-training using widely available datasets like ImageNet is a commonly employed tactic 
to achieve this, as it enables models to develop essential skills before proceeding 
with more complex specific mission objectives, such as semantic segmentation. 
ImageNet's classification dataset consists of diverse natural scenes, whereas 
semantic segmentation focuses on parsing individual scene components. 
Recent research suggests that depth estimation using a single camera can 
complement these image datasets by imparting three-dimensional scene understanding. 
In this study, we evaluate the efficacy of depth estimation as a pre-training 
objective for semantic segmentation. Notably, we observed that models trained with 
depth estimation as a pre-training task in conjunction with classification 
performed best when evaluated on tasks requiring three-dimensional inference. 
Moreover, models pre-trained with depth estimation exhibited improved adaptability 
when adapting to new outdoor datasets. However, when evaluating models on 
three-dimensional tasks that might not necessitate pre-training with depth 
estimation, as well as when evaluating models on specific segmentation tasks, 
models pre-trained using classification performed slightly better. As such, we 
advocate for a mixed pre-training approach that incorporates a variety of training 
objectives, as their relative effectiveness might vary depending on specific task 
requirements. Valuable insights were gained through experimenting with pre-training

On a Cayley tree, we analyze the Ising model and find novel Gibbs measures that exhibit mild periodicity. These measures are derived from interconnecting multiple Ising models, each defined on a separate Cayley tree with different temperatures. As a result, the system's phase transitions are prevented, yet we demonstrate the existence of unique temperature values where the system's free energy achieves a maximum or minimum value. Conversely, our findings indicate that the system's thermodynamic limit yields the standard Gibbs measure, commonly seen in statistical mechanics. Furthermore, our work expands upon previous research conducted by Byrska and Gralak, published in 1989, where similar measures were explored on a single Cayley tree. Crucially, our study reveals the stationary distribution of a time-evolving Ising model, which exhibits ergodic behavior, thereby addressing a long-standing open problem first posed by Dobrushin in the 1970s. In federated learning, multiple parties collaborate on training machine learning models by sharing local parameters, rather than sensitive data. While this approach minimizes data exposure, it is still vulnerable to hacking, particularly when training models. A novel combination of techniques, encompassing OPAE-based Trusted Execution Environments, P2P communication, and Mixture of Experts, has been integrated into a framework called flatee. This framework effectively secures federated training against malicious attacks by involving a TEE, thereby preventing access to model parameters and data, thus preventing reversal engineering and model extraction attacks. As a result, the model's weight updates are the only shared information, thereby protecting against data exposure. This paper introduces a novel approach called Timeloops, automated system call filtering, to tackle the challenges posed by the complex system calls of containerized microservices. The incorporation of containers revolutionized application deployment but failed to address the security vulnerabilities associated with microservices' extensive system call requirements. Inspired by similar problems, Timeloops leverages techniques from access control policy learning, combining machine learning and rule-based systems to create a dynamic, adaptable filter. By learning from experience, Timeloops generates a time-agnostic system call policy, eliminating the need for static policy frameworks. Furthermore, Timeloops' analytical capabilities enable runtime discovery and visualization of policy infringements, facilitating security audit trails, anomaly detection, and security informatics. The performance of Timeloops, specifically its potential vulnerabilities, is evaluated through a diverse set of microservices benchmarking suite, Benchmark for Containerized Microservices (BCM). The experimental findings demonstrate that Timeloops achieves a competitive performance, both in training and deployment, supplanting existing system call filtering methods. Moreover, Timeloops' efficacy in various deployment scenarios, encompassing different filter architectures and benchmark services, is consistently evident. The source code of Timeloops is freely available at github.com/eclipse/flowVis to foster community engagement and further development. The EMP chain (https://github.com/EclipseEmpirical/EMP_chain) including Timeloops, together with the corresponding technical report, can be found at arxiv.org/abs/2205.04173. Additionally, the research artifacts, comprising data, design, and implementation details, are made available at researchware.org/project/flowVis. This work investigates how second-order logic with quantification over sets and functions translates to first-order logic with quantification over pairs, when dealing with dual relations. Ultimately, we demonstrate that first-order model theory with dual relations is equivalent to second-order model theory with sets and functions. The findings of the investigation reveal that the influence of quantum uncertainty on the horizon of the polymer black hole manifests as a displacement in the radius of the event horizon, which in turn affects the quasinormal mode frequencies. Notably, the paper discovers that the influence of quantum uncertainty on the radius of the event horizon is dependent on the spin of the scalar field, with the relationship being linear for non-zero spin cases and quadratic for the case of a scalar field with zero spin. Recent advances in voice conversion using sequence-to-sequence models have achieved significant improvements. However, these models struggle with speech degradation, particularly when attempting to change speaking styles. This issue can be addressed by incorporating a masking technique that filters out irrelevant information from the speaker's identity. While the masking technique has been explored in voice conversion, its potential applications extend beyond this domain. This study investigates the use of the masking technique in speech synthesis and evaluates its effectiveness in controlling speaking styles. Moreover, we developed a dialog-based dataset to examine the effects of the masking techniques on speech generation. Our experimental results indicate that the masking technique can successfully reduce speech degradation and enhance voice conversion performance. Additionally, our analysis suggests that using a dialogue prompt instead of a speaker's previous speech as input to a neural network synthesizer produces high-quality outputs with reduced speech degradation. Our research shows promising results that could benefit natural dialogue systems, particularly in controlling speech characteristics through masking. The code for this research is available on the GitHub repository: https://github.com/ChiaChingHsu/MaskedDialogue.

Advancements in deep learning technology, particularly data augmentation techniques, have led to greater accuracy in model training. Nonetheless, the reliance on user-provided data for augmentation remains a challenge, as adversaries can exploit this vulnerability in machine learning models by launching Person-in-the-Middle (MitM) attacks. Through malicious manipulation of training data, adversaries can successfully perturb models, rendering them susceptible to manipulation and attack. In this research, we identify the vulnerabilities in the training process of neural networks and explore the feasibility of launching MitM attacks on machine learning models trained using the Adversarial Training method via generative frameworks. An experiment was conducted to evaluate the effectiveness of Adversarial Training models against internal and external adversaries, as well as against models generated using the Normalizing Flows and GAN frameworks. Our findings indicate that adversarial training can provide robustness against certain types of attacks; however, the use of generative models may introduce new vulnerabilities to machine learning models. An open-source code for this research is available at https://github.com/JAIST-VIG/person-in-the-middle-attacks. Climate denial narratives spread rapidly through social media, driving the dissemination of misleading information about climate change. We have identified a type of climate denial narrative which claims that certain groups are intentionally manipulating climate data, and attribute this manipulation to specific entities such as governments or organizations. This is the first study to comprehensively analyze these 'conspiracy theory' narratives, focusing on their core elements, dissemination via social media and associated stakeholders, as well as the impact they have on the broader public discourse surrounding climate change. We utilize a unique combination of natural language processing, extensive media corpus analysis and online dataset, allowing for an in-depth exploration of this particular climate denial narrative and its distinct characteristics. Our findings also reveal that this conspiracy theory primarily targets domain-external groups such as governments and organizations, and is particularly prevalent on platforms like Parler and Gab, where it often feeds into a broader discourse of political polarization. We propose multiple avenues for future research, primarily focusing on the relationship between climate denial narratives and political polarization as well as the efficacy of counter-narratives targeted at addressing this conspiracy theory. Our research could also be replicated to investigate denial narratives centered on other contentious topics. Code for this research is publicly hosted on GitHub at https://github.com/jjy1123/Climate-Conspiracy-Theories. Zhiyan Jiang, Junho Shin, and Jisun Cheng contributed equally to this work.

Instrumental variable estimation is typically applied under the assumption of a single deterministic treatment, yet in fields like education, individuals are often exposed to a variety of treatments. We present a new model incorporating multiple treatment variables with uncertain selection, drawing on data from fields of study as an empirical example. A key identification condition for this context involves the reliance on specific subspaces of treatment options, leading to the adoption of the term 'instrumental space'. We utilize data from fields of study to estimate its effects on earnings by taking into account varying levels of college major diversity, utilizing a statistical method called Bayesian structural identification. Our analysis reveals that, ceteris paribus, college majors diversifying beyond STEM fields and social sciences yield greater earnings than arts and humanities. Additionally, this research offers a framework for assessing the causal influence of uncertain treatments, providing a metric for the probability of active participation in certain treatment subspaces and establishing a relationship with the concept of causal "skewness". Finally, our study illustrates the utility of a particular college major diversity metric in yielding finite and relevant causal estimates, thus providing a practical means of instrumental variable selection. A companion online appendix supplements this analysis with supplementary content.

A solar type I noise storm is created by particle beams interacting with the Sun's photosphere and lower chromosphere, producing millihertz continuums and radio bursts of various types. Introducing an atom positioned in front of a mirror, our analysis explores how the atom's movement induces electromagnetic emissions when it moves towards or away from the mirror, and this emission process can be modeled using a confined space capacitor system. Derived from this setup, our model calculates the electromagnetic radiation emitted by the atom, and specifically, how its acceleration affects the emission process. Notably, our results demonstrate that the atom can radiate energy even when it's not in its ground state, and this emission process relies on the atom's movement as well as the interaction between the atom and mirror. Introducing a mirror with a groove, our model also considers the case of an atom situated within the groove, and as a result, the atom experiences an additional movement due to the groove's confinement. In this situation, the atom can become polarized, and upon moving, it generates a varying electric dipole moment that gives rise to electromagnetic radiation. This general approach holds the promise for further exploring the interaction between atoms and curved surfaces as a source of new technological innovations. often suffer from poor color representation due to outdated printing techniques.
Monochrome images were typically presented with imaginary colors to convey information
about brightness and color using colored overlays. These overlays have faded over time,
leaving present-day scans with low color resolution and limited dynamic range. Our goal
is to restore and enhance historical astronomical photographs by improving color,
while maintaining existing features. We propose a solution involving Generative Adversarial
Networks, specifically the Style Transfer and Generative Adversarial Training methods, to
achieve high-quality results. Our approach demonstrates success in color restoration and
enhancement, particularly for images with low resolution and limited color information. We
also examine the performance of transfer learning in this application. Additionally, we
created a public colorization dataset for astronomical images, which can be utilized for

We propose a novel neural network architecture whose backpropagation is unnecessary, instead relying on a simplified non-linear regression method to optimize connections. This framework maintains the same level of data interpretation as traditional neural networks and has the advantage of reduced computational complexity. Additionally, we have modified the network to incorporate the Universal Approximation Theorem, enabling us to achieve desired network outputs with any level of accuracy. Furthermore, we have developed an algorithm to determine the optimal number of hidden layers and neurons required to achieve a specified level of approximation within a given dataset. This algorithm is based on analyzing the information complexity of the dataset. We have successfully implemented this new architecture in solving various regression and classification problems with different data sets, including both synthetic and real-world data, and have obtained highly satisfactory results. We have also compared our new framework with other state-of-the-art models, including support vector machines and kernel ridge regression, and have found it to consistently outperform these models across a range of experiments. We have investigated the phenomenon of line waves within a dual metastructure and its applications in guiding electromagnetic waves. The theoretical model we employed to analyze the line waves resonances matches the resonances observed in experimental data collected using scanning near-field optical microscopy. By modifying the line waves resonances using varying line widths at the edges of perforations, we observed changes in resonance frequencies. The resonances can potentially be adjusted to align with the dual phase, promoting high efficiency transmission in bidirectional optical devices. Furthermore, controlling line widths could enable independent adjustment of line waves and the dual phase's characteristics, offering flexibility in designing optical functions. The study's findings offer new avenues for the development of guided photonics. The concept of line waves resonances could also be explored in other fields, such as acoustic photonics. The theoretical model analyzed in this study can be translated to other photonics systems, and the observed line waves resonances can be tuned through modifications in line widths to achieve desired optical functions. The task of relation extraction aims to derive factual relationships from textual data, with widely-used benchmarks like TAC-KBP relying heavily on annotated datasets. However, extracting and labeling such data is extremely resource-intensive, prompting research into pre-trained models like BERT. While pre-trained models have shown significant potential in relation extraction, their ability to capture long-range dependencies and adapt to various domains has yet to be fully leveraged. Building on the success of link prediction in knowledge graph completion, researchers have integrated additional knowledge graphs into relation extraction models. Notably, using generic knowledge graphs has been shown to hinder sector-specific extraction, like protein-related information. In response, we've developed a novel strategy involving tailored knowledge graphs for relation extraction, especially those within the biology sector. By doing so, we've established a method to effectively exploit these tailored knowledge graphs and improve the models' capacity for link prediction, ultimately driving enhanced performance in relation extraction. In particular, we've explored various approaches to create sector-specific knowledge graphs for relation extraction, including one based on word embeddings and another based on knowledge graph embedding. We've successfully implemented these methods in the context of the TAC-KBP challenge, achieving a 11.01 F1 score in the biology category using our proposed strategy. In comparison, this approach outperformed a BERT-only model by a 3.5 F1 point margin, solidifying its potential as a reliable and efficient method to enhance relation extraction using knowledge graphs. The code for this research is available on GitHub at https://github.com/jjyang1994/SEKG4RE. Experimental results demonstrate that our strategy can serve as a basic model for relation extraction, serving to close the gap between pre-trained models and knowledge-based approaches. Notably, we've found that our strategy can be effectively used to augment knowledge-based models, while also providing a potential pathway to train data-less models for relation extraction. Furthermore, we've investigated its applicability to other biology datasets and the results indicate its potential in improving performance when sector-specific knowledge graphs are available. In summary, we've established a method to integrate tailored knowledge graphs for relation extraction, specifically within biology, and demonstrated its potential in enhancing performance, while also exploring its potential in data-less models and other biology datasets. In a simple grid-based game where players attempt to remove tiles from a board to get to the zero area, strategies vary widely. A strategy is considered successful if playing it allows one player to win the game. To determine successful strategies, we define key elements: specific tile values that must appear in the game and specific locations where they must appear. Building on prior research, we create a set of essential strategies which form the foundation for all other successful strategies. By breaking down each strategy into its grid pattern and the associated grid minima, we can compare and classify different tactics. Although some grid minima are already understood, many more need to be explored. With over 35 new grid minima identified, we add to the existing knowledge and pave the way for further study in this game. Additionally, we introduce an open-source mathematical software package for computing grid minima, making it available for public use. By defining a measure for grid complexity, we prioritize the computation of grid minima for low complexity values first. After establishing a set of reference grids, which are the grid minima for low complexity values, we demonstrate how our method can efficiently compute grid minima even for very large game boards. As a result, we are able to find a grid minimum for the 13x13 board and show that it can be extended to solve the game for tiles with values up to six, while also showcasing its applications in solving other simple grid-based games. With this research, we open the door for further developments in computing grid minima and showcase the potential for these developments by applying them to other areas of mathematics. Furthermore, we reveal a connection between grid minima and a long-standing mathematical problem, specifically the strong infinity conjecture in combinatorial geometry, which has gone unsolved for over 20 years. Based on our computation of grid minima, we provide a partial solution, proving the infinity conjecture for a significant case. To show the breadth of our method, applying which yields new results and insights, we explore three diverse scenarios where grid minima can be utilized: simplifying machine learning-based game solutions, enhancing the performance of search algorithms, and extending the limits of what can be achieved in game theory. In summary, we have developed a powerful computational tool for grid minima, which has numerous applications across different fields, and made notable advancements in solving the infinity conjecture and understanding game strategy grids. Specifically, we'll outline a new approach to deriving meaningful features from ML models, utilizing a layer-wise relevance calculation through backwards tracing, based on the data-driven connections identified by an ML model. This approach forms the foundation of a new ML model interpretation framework, incorporating expert knowledge, effectively merging human and AI-driven feature selection capabilities. To demonstrate its efficacy, we'll apply this method to a high-energy physics dataset, focusing on jet identification, where feature importance from an ML model is used to create a new set of expert variables, incorporating intricate physical rules, to train an additional ML model. Moreover, incorporating the new set of expert variables onto the original ML model further enhances its accuracy, highlighting the benefits of combining human and AI-driven feature selection capabilities. In the sign problem, Monte Carlo simulations face an obstacle due to an inherent exponential explosion of complex weights in importance sampling, especially when addressing lattice Quantum Field Theories like QCD and many-body Hamiltonians like the Hubbard model. We introduce a solution to the sign problem by utilizing complex-valued neural networks as an efficient tool for importance sampling. By representing complex weights with a real-valued layer followed by a complex-valued activation function, we prevent exponential explosions and thus overcome the sign dilemma. Our innovative approach successfully achieves reasonable results for the three-dimensional SU(3) gauge theory and the Hubbard model, especially in extremely harsh conditions. Additionally, when compared to phase transformation methods, our approach shows more flexibility and a greater potential for improvement. Furthermore, our analysis indicates that the complex-valued activation function plays a crucial role in determining the performance of the network. Finally, our work also serves as a proof of concept that neural networks can serve as a versatile tool for addressing the sign problem in a broad range of quantum systems. Nonetheless, a significant challenge still lies in developing networks that can efficiently learn from data, rather than being trained through a tedious trial-and-error process. Fortunately, our study also paves the way for future research in this area, specifically in understanding how to efficiently train networks using quantum data. According to our findings, the sign problem can be efficiently overcome when the network learns to integrate importance sampling weights over multiple steps, rather than at the initial level. This discovery marks an important breakthrough in the development of neural network-based solutions to the sign problem and extends our previous work on the Hubbard model to a more complex quantum system like the SU(3) gauge theory. Ultimately, our innovative approach may accelerate the computation of Monte Carlo simulations, thus paving the way for a future breakthrough in our understanding of quantum systems. To verify our claims, we developed and implemented a novel, efficient network architecture for the importance sampling weights, specifically tailored to a complex-valued structure. Our analysis demonstrates that this network surpasses previous results and opens up new avenues for addressing the sign problem. Moreover, our work directly compares our signs problem solution to previous transformation methods, highlighting both the strengths and the limitations of these approaches in both 2D and 3D simulations. To showcase our results, we presented a detailed analysis of our novel neural network architecture in both 2D and 3D simulations, emphasizing its efficient structure and remarkable performance. In a composite Higgs model, where $SU(6)/Sp(6)$ is used, the flavor symmetry is identified as an $U(1)$ subgroup of $Sp(6)$. Here, the complex scalar field's', acting as a pseudo-Nambu-Goldstone boson, plays the role of a flavon, which bears a flavor charge. Upon the VEV of the flavon, $U(1)_F$ flavor symmetry is broken. This break results in the emergence of a small parameter and consequently generates a hierarchy between top and bottom quark masses. A flavon lighter than the TeV scale can naturally be introduced, which makes it a completely testable model to understand the origins of hierarchical quark masses. Furthermore, an interesting aspect is that this flavon can also contribute to the $b\rightarrow s\mu^{+}\mu^{-}$ process. A study using the SU(3)C and SU(2)_L gauge symmetries shows that this theory is consistent with several constraints. This research delves into the concept of unverified assumptions in software development. Unverified assumptions are unsubstantiated presumptions made by software engineers regarding how users will interact with their programs. Our investigation involves analyzing unverified assumptions through a framework that identifies them, understands their origins, and evaluates the risks posed by these assumptions. This analysis reveals that a substantial portion of unverified assumptions lack formal validation despite being critical to program functionality. Our study also reveals that tackling unverified assumptions via just-in-time (JIT) compilers offers a promising avenue for improvement. JIT compilers generate machine code at runtime using techniques such as decompilation, speculation, and transformation. By drawing on concepts from clausal learning, we are developing a prototype framework called CLADA that utilizes decompilation and speculative execution to probe unverified assumptions at runtime. CLADA's approach learns from its surroundings, detects unverified assumptions in use cases, and performs empirical risk assessments - all without necessitating human intervention. CLADA's framework comprises three components: unverified assumption detection, empirical risk assessment, and a learning mechanism. Our experimental findings with Python unverified assumptions suggest that CLADA effectively detects, assesses risks of, and learns from unverified assumptions, thereby reducing risks without requiring user input. CLADA's performance compares favorably to existing methods, with its strengths centered around improved efficiency and enhanced robustness. Notably, CLADA detects 50% of unverified assumptions at runtime that developers previously overlooked. At the time of writing, CLADA's prototype has not encountered any false positives. We intend to expand CLADA to encompass various programming languages and challenge its efficacy in detecting unverified assumptions within its specified scope. CLADA's potential lies in reducing risks posed by unverified assumptions across a range of programs. To facilitate CLADA's adoption, we plan to make its prototype framework open-source, enabling users to experiment with CLADA and evaluate its performance on diverse programs. Our ultimate goal is to empower developers to safely explore unverified assumptions in software development, thereby expanding the reach of current programming techniques. In the process, we strive to empower developers to confidently make educated guesses and explore new frontiers in programming. We aim for CLADA to empower developers to courageously push the boundaries of what is considered safe in software development. Ultimately, we aim for CLADA to serve as a pioneering model for learning unverified assumptions that empowers developers to boldly venture into uncharted territories of program functionality. CLADA's future iterations may lead to the development of tools monitoring unverified assumptions at runtime and providing alerts

Ultimately, our method's high accuracy and scalability make it an ideal solution for instantaneous incident identification across vast areas and timescales. This study investigates the benefits of relinquishing cross-entropy for binary and multi-class classification. Our analysis involves comparing a comprehensive set of modified loss functions across various datasets, and we examine the regularisation effects, training stability, and model performance to understand how our choices impact neural networks. Furthermore, we tie these observations back to the fundamental mathematical properties of these loss functions. Our aim is to equip developers with a clear understanding of the advantages and limitations of altering cross-entropy for classification tasks. Additionally, our open-source code and comprehensive benchmarking study against state-of-the-art benchmarks using the FLOPS metric are intended to facilitate the reproduction of our findings for further investigation. By pushing the boundaries of current loss functions, our work aims to stimulate innovative research in deep learning that is both efficient and effective. Overall, our findings reveal that, under specific conditions, relinquishing cross-entropy leads to superior performance, faster model training, and enhanced generalisation, albeit with increased computational complexity. Specifically, our investigations into binary loss functions show that leveraging the Kullback-Leibler divergence yields superior results; in contrast, our exploration of classification loss functions suggests the utilisation of the sharpness-regulated label-corrected cross-entropy for improved model performance and training stability when working with labelled pseudo-output data. Our analyses also uncover a connection between regularisation, training stability, and the loss function's Lipschitz constant, which guides future research on the practical applications of regularisation and training stability. Ultimately, our study seeks to bridge the gap between efficient machine learning algorithms and practical deep learning methods by validating hypotheses that are currently unprovable in the context of well-established loss functions. To this end, our work presents a comprehensive evaluation of binary and multi-class classification loss functions, encompassing novel variants of the Kullback-Leiberg divergence, label-corrected cross-entropy, and neighbourhood components analysis, which possess desirable mathematical properties and exhibit superior performance in comparison to cross-entropy. Our analysis also examines the effectiveness of these loss functions across diverse datasets and training conditions, which sheds light on the underlying connections between regularisation, training stability, and the loss function's Lipschitz constant, and could potentially guide the development of future efficient deep learning algorithms. Approximations are introduced, leading to a simplified model known as the extended RPA framework. While the RPA is analogous to a particle-like condition, it introduces artifacts such as overestimation of static responses and inability to capture fluctuations below a certain threshold. Conversely, the RPA's counterpart, the memory-loss approximation, yields inaccurate results for interactions stronger than a certain threshold and fails to capture fluctuations below this threshold. Ultimately, the xRPA family, consisting of the RPA and its extensions, including the memory-loss approximation and higher-order extensions, can be understood through the lens of Hamiltonian-based model development. Furthermore, a novel, fourth-order extension to the parquet approach is proposed, addressing the parquet's susceptibility discontinuity and enabling a description of fluctuations at any order of the coupling constant. Nonetheless, the fourth-order extension incurs an expansion deficit in comparison to the xRPA family and may benefit from additional corrections in the weak-coupling regime. Additionally, a fourth-order extension to the RPA-based description of spinless Fermi systems is proposed, with potential extensions to Fermi systems with spin. Despite its spinless nature, this fourth-order description is tied to a fully interacting Hamiltonian with inherent signs, analogous to certain models of lattice-based interacting spin systems. In both the strong- and weak-coupling regimes, fourth-order corrections to the RPA are effectively captured by this new description. Furthermore, a similar fourth-order framework can be developed for the p-p approximation, with potential extensions to the parquet approach. Lastly, a fourth-order extension to the RPA-based description of optical responses is proposed, with potential generalizations to the parquet approach and descriptions of electronic responses beyond the linear approximation. This novel approach allows us to introduce a new type of attractive interaction and achieves a level of methodological sophistication previously unseen. Utilizing the technique, we have analyzed the phase diagram of single-layer TiSe2 and demonstrated the occurrence of exciton liquefaction near the Fermi point. Our calculations also reveal that the material undergoes exciton hydrodynamic behavior, leading to the expansion of the lattice and the activation of long-wave-length phonons. Conversely, we have found that electron liquefaction is not realized in TiSe2 due to the influence of lattice vibrations. Lastly, we have observed that the Mott transition, exciton liquefaction, and superconductivity in TiSe2 are interlinked phenomena. Ultimately, this study paves the groundwork for the generation of ultra-high temperature superconductors through the strategy of exciton liquefaction. Additionally, it also holds promise for the creation of new states of matter through the phase transition of quantum fluids. Lastly, it also offers an innovative approach to simulating quantum field theories using a digital platform. This paper presents an analysis of a text-based reporting system used by community members and reveals the hidden patterns in their interactions with the dispatchers. Despite the importance of these interactions, comprehensive knowledge about them is lacking due to the hidden nature of their conversation. To uncover these hidden patterns, a dataset of 889 real-world reports was collected, along with the dispatchers' responses, from a community reporting system. This dataset facilitated the development of multiple text-oriented approaches for identifying recurring user inquiries and the dispatchers' standard responses. Notably, the proposed methods demonstrated superior performance compared to other existing methods, yielding higher accuracy and a broader discovery range of relevant interactions. The analysis of these interactions provides dispatchers with insights to improve their responses, while also informing system designers of effective questioning strategies to enhance the system's overall effectiveness. The findings of this study can provide valuable insights for designers and their users, leading to a better understanding of how to design effective text-based systems, as well as how to engage with users through natural language interactions. The proposed models and analysis provide a foundation for exploring the concealed insights of human interactions within larger contexts, as seen in the community security setting. To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped CeCu$_2$De in a nematic superconducting state, we computationally investigate how the couples' spin interacts with an applied magnetic field. When the field's orientation polymorphism is considered, Pauli paramagnetism becomes noticeably present in a limited wavevector space, distinct from its quasiparticle and condensate components. In contrast, the coupled spins within the Cooper couples do not significantly contribute to this paramagnetism. Additionally, as interlayer long-range pairing increases through doping, the couples' spin interaction via the Luke-Nobel effect diminishes significantly. This is consistent with experimental observations on CeCu$_2$De where a transition from a antiferromagnetic to a nematic superconducting state is witnessed upon doping. Furthermore, the study reveals another novel phase where interlayer $\ell=1$ and $\ell=2$ pairing coexist, driven by Fermi surface fragmentation and coupling, respectively. In this phase, Fermi surface fragments that are paired with $\ell=1$ respond paramagnetically to applied magnetization, while $\ell=2$ paired entities do not, unlike in a purely nematic superconducting state. The computational model employed is based on the minimal model proposed by Haas et al. for CeCu$_2$De, where strong coupling to this material is reflected in a highly scaled Fermi surface. By treating its parameters as highly sensitive to Fermi surface size and shape, the study provides an analytical bridge to a recent review on highly correlated metals by Pines et al. where a distinct type of "orphaned" quantum criticality is described. The computational model was solved using Green function technique, resulting in a three-dimensional frequency and wavevector-dependent spectral density, along with first-order many-body coupled equations for interlayer long-range pairing. In this context, Fermi surface properties are viewed as inherently bound to superconducting ones, essentially making Fermi surface physics a byproduct of understanding these processes. The study therefore marks a significant departure from purely quantum critical investigations, instead emphasizing a crucial role for Fermi surface in driving nematic superconductivity. The findings could also provide a theoretical foundation for further experimental research on nematic superconductors like CeCu$_2$De and related materials like FeSe. We introduce a new paradigm for computer vision tasks called minimax engaged learning, which offers flexible choices for processing mechanisms, allowing users to specify the competitive nature of models for a more precise computation of the game-theoretic solution. A key challenge in computer vision has been resolving the equilibrium of adversarial networks, primarily due to the lack of effective optimization methods. To address this issue, our approach starts by identifying a theoretical bound on the cost of adversarial training. This calculation demonstrates that the outcome of adversarial training is close to the minimax engaged learning solution under certain conditions. Building upon this insight, we develop a majorization-minorization algorithm to solve the adversarial network problem. The proposed method makes successive approximations to the game-theoretic solution by iteratively improving both the player and the opponent strategies. We test the efficacy of our approach on various vision tasks, including multi-task learning with adversarial regularizer, image segmentation, and image generation. The experiments show that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques. The integration of game-theoretic models with deep learning has given rise to a new and powerful training paradigm known as minimax engaged learning, enabling the computation of equilibrium points in learning games. The theoretical foundations for this approach involve deriving bounds on the cost of adversarial training and describing novel training algorithms for dependent models. These foundations, based on majorization-minorization principles, allow for the evaluation of training dynamics and the optimization of dependent models. The efficacy of our method has been demonstrated through applications to image denoising and generation. The impact of our work includes novel connections between training dynamics and equilibrium points, as well as the extension of training paradigms beyond alternating player methods. The empirical evaluations show that our approach outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques in various vision tasks. Furthermore, the obtained results provide insights into the dynamics of training processes and the quality of generated images. The proposed minimax engaged learning paradigm offers flexible choices for processing mechanisms and enables the efficient training of dependent models. The study's contributions include novel algorithms for the equilibrium solution and empirical evaluations of generated image quality. In a experimental setup where a series of tasks are completed and their results monitored, researchers utilize multiple-entry reinforcement scheduling (MERS) to adapt to a dynamic environment. MERS is a theoretical model that is demonstrated through simulation using a context in which a brain region, akin to the striatum, responds to the completion of tasks with varying degrees of reward. By applying this model to simulated data, researchers observed that it produces signatures reminiscent of long-term depression (LTD) observed in neural activity. Through simulation, two distinct patterns of adaptation were identified - slow and fast - which were both found to be persistent forms of adaptation. Additionally, the results suggest that the fast adaptation could be the result of a neurobiological mechanism involving the activation of NMDA receptors followed by a subsequent inhibitory response. Furthermore, the observations from the simulations were found to be consistent with empirical findings from human neuroimaging studies. The study demonstrates that MERS can effectively generate data that reflects real-world neurobiological processes involved in adaptation. In the past, AI courses centered around solving real-world problems, but current trends emphasize exploring AI's potential as a means to enhance learning. This transformation prompts an inquiry into how we can incorporate computational elements into educational content that was traditionally presented in a dry, theoretical manner. In this study, we examine the applicability of a user-friendly AI-powered platform for creating customized, interactive content, based on a prior analysis of its technical applications and evaluations involving novice researchers. Our findings indicate that the platform can be utilized to develop a wide range of computational tools, and that generating these tools is a enjoyable, creative experience. Additionally, the study reveals that the platform's capabilities extend beyond the boundaries of the research group and can be applied to various domains such as harmonic analysis. It is anticipated that the research will facilitate more playful and creative approaches to teaching AI, by highlighting the platform's versatility and its potential to inspire new, computational elements. The study also presents a collection of 20 interactive experiments developed using the platform, and serves as a resource for those seeking to apply the method and reproduce the results. A rapidly evolving environment necessitates efficient reward learning for robotic systems to adapt to unfamiliar settings quickly. Under these conditions, traditional methods using state observations alone are insufficient to learn an effective reward function. To address this challenge, we propose a solution that leverages both visual and auditory cues to facilitate reward learning through comparison and categorization. By processing sensory input and output from human evaluations, our approach adapts a reinforcement learning agent's objective function, thereby enhancing the agent's decision-making capabilities. To optimize this process and reduce human effort, we develop an online clustering technique based on information gained from human feedback. As a result, the agent is able to prioritize areas with higher human evaluation rates and merge sensory input from related sources. Our proposed method demonstrates time-effective reward learning capabilities through simulations involving complex, high-dimensional settings. Additionally, we showcase applications and evaluations using actual robots for scenarios like navigating to unknown locations and determining the state of a door. Our results indicate that these visual aids significantly enhance the agent's ability to define objectives and achieve successful task outcomes. This study examines the scenario in which multiple co-rotating vortex rings in an ideal 2D fluid move towards each other in a highly collaborative and organized manner, ultimately resulting in the precise creation of a thin bridge connecting the merging vortex rings and preserving the overall area within the enclosed space. The key features of this process involve the emergence of a self-similar pattern at high speeds and a complex interplay of geometric and analytic principles in the resulting bridge's shape. The study also proves a long-standing conjecture in this field first proposed by Levine and co-workers in 1983. The analysis uses a specific type of flow called Schrödinger operators and the theory of majorizing measures to convey the highly organized and predictable nature of this physical scenario. The work has been published in the journal Annals of Mathematics. A corresponding video demonstrating the predicted shape of the bridge is also available online. The research was partially funded by ANR-14-CE25-0019 and ERC-2020-LQUIDS. The funding sources are the French Agence Nationale de la Recherche and the European Research Council, respectively. The abstract of the paper may be translated as follows: In a highly structured two-dimensional fluid system, an old mathematical problem related to vortex rings has been solved. The solution reveals that as these vortex rings interact and move towards each other in a controlled and organized way, they will always find a critical speed at which they will merge and preserve the enclosed area within the space they occupy. The critical speed makes the bridge connecting the vortex rings as thin as the speed of sound, and the shape of the bridge preserves the original features of the space they occupy. The study also proves that this critical speed will always be higher than the speed of sound, and the shape of the bridge will always be different from the original space they occupy. The solution relies on a complex mathematical theory, and the expression of the bridge is connected to a highly complex mathematical operator called Schrödinger operators. The study also emerges from a significant research in the field of vortex rings interaction that was led by Thomas Levine in 1983. The analysis does not provide any practical application for the prediction of the bridge's shape, but it rather showcases the highly organized and predictable nature of this physical scenario. A cutting-edge technique known as Enhanced Inverse Probability Weighting (EIPW) has significantly improved the accuracy of predicting long-term outcomes in medical settings. Building upon EIPW, we introduce a modified version called Standardized Enhanced Inverse Probability Weighting (SIPW) that uses neural network forecasts. Unlike EIPW, which uses actual observed data to calculate weighting factors, SIPW employs a standardized version to eliminate potential biases. Experimental findings with a dataset from US hospitals reveal that SIPW yields more precise predictions compared to EIPW, as well as a substantial improvement in model stability using bootstrap resampling methods. Furthermore, the analysis demonstrates that SIPW's advantages are more pronounced in datasets with (1) a smaller follow-up period, (2) higher censoring rates, and (3) broader prediction intervals. Hence, SIPW is an effective technique for enhancing risk prediction, particularly under specific data conditions. A typical strategy for modeling extreme events involves considering occurrences beyond a high threshold as events of a non-homogeneous Poisson process. Specifically, we utilize the changes of variables in both the likelihood and its posterior, obtaining a significant simplification. Consequently, closed-form approximations can be derived for mean and median posterior predictions of future excess losses. Our method is demonstrated using a case study of maximum daily rainfall in London. The results show substantial reductions in computational time, allowing for the generation of precise posterior predictions within a reasonable time frame. As a direct result, we obtain the optimal L^2-controllability in a short time frame for this system using only surface controls, and further expand upon this to achieve interior controls based on minimal time estimates via a standard calculus of variations approach. This paper reveals that there are two primary categories of out-of-domain text: one category consists of text that contradicts the expected format or contains irrelevant information, and the other category comprises text that lacks a clear domain opposition but nonetheless deviates from the expected format. Interestingly, a model trained on in-domain text alone can effectively identify texts that clearly contradict the expected format, but performance significantly deteriorates when confronted with texts that lack a clear domain opposition. To address this challenge, we have developed two novel out-of-domain detection methods: one method involves assessing text coherence and adherence to a predicted class-based structure, and the other method leverages the similarity between generated and real-world text pairs. Notably, this method requires no pair-wise training and can be implemented using an autoencoder. Our proposed method exceeds the performance of prior techniques, and our analysis also offers insight into why models trained solely on in-domain text may struggle with out-of-domain text detection. Our method can be particularly beneficial in tasks such as text generation, filtering, and classification. To accurately analyze complex systems, it is essential to distinguish between smooth variations and abrupt changes. In the context of machine learning, this translates to differentiating between predictable patterns and unforeseen events. Inspired by this challenge, a novel approach called Linear and Nonlinear Disambiguation Optimization (LANDO) has been developed. LANDO utilizes kernel regression to identify patterns in high-dimensional data, while minimizing the influence of outliers and abrupt changes. By applying a dynamic background learning method, LANDO is able to effectively handle abrupt changes and maintain accurate predictions. Furthermore, by using a sparse approximation, LANDO is capable of operating in low-dimensional spaces, making it suitable for data analysis in large-dimensional systems. The efficacy of LANDO has been demonstrated through a variety of numerical simulations, including a study of turbulent flows and image degradation. The algorithm's success highlights the importance of robust pattern identification in data analysis, particularly in contexts where outliers and abrupt changes occur. The diverse range of chess openings has been a subject of both individual and collective exploration by players and analysts for centuries, with recent decades seeing the emergence of sophisticated computer-based approaches to study them, often grounded in abstract chess principles and technical puzzles. This research leverages a massive online chess dataset to quantify the complexity and similarity of over 800,000 distinct opening variations, revealing a scale-free network in which more popular openings cluster together and less popular ones are dispersed. This empirical framework can be compared to other cultural evolution studies and provides a data-driven foundation for a deeper understanding of the evolution of chess openings. Furthermore, this analysis sheds light on the challenges of extracting concepts from digital data and highlights the significance of crowdsourced content in forming collective memories. Finally, this research paves the way for the application of social network analysis to other online knowledge domains.

These algorithms leverage parameterized techniques to efficiently manage the complexity of DAGs by exploiting promising layouts of underlying undirected graphs.
