A snake-like robot has evolved from inspiring robotics literature, with research focusing on undulatory movements. Although theories based on the central nervous system's simplified models have been developed, they have not been thoroughly tested on undulatory robots. This work proposes a novel, neurologically grounded climbing gait, inspired by eels, which incorporates their unique movement patterns. This movement pattern allows robots to navigate through tight spaces by moving forward while maintaining position. Prior research has only explored this gait in simulated environments; we experiment with evaluating this gait in both simulated and real environments using a snake robot. The results show that the eel-inspired movement pattern allows the robot to climb vertical planes with success rates higher than other movements, even in real-world experiments. Additionally, we found that the eel-inspired movement outperforms other movements when the distance to the target is short. To validate these findings, a large-scale simulation with various environments was conducted. The eel-inspired movement was found to be more effective than other movements, with the discrepancy between simulated and real-world results due to the imperfections in the simulation. The introduction of imperfections in the simulation led to the unexpected discovery that the eel-inspired movement could fail at times, which isn't observed in real-world experiments. The reason behind this could be the oversimplification of the movement model. Based on these findings, we suggest potential future research directions. Possible applications for this research could be in search and rescue operations or other scenarios where undulatory movements could be beneficial. The code for the simulation is publicly available on GitHub. The snake robot used in the real-world experiments is owned by Kevin Myers; if there's any interest in repeating the experiment, please contact him at kevin.myers@sheffield.ac.uk. The eel-inspired movement, which can be found on github.com/kevinmyers/snake-robot-eel-inspiration, could potentially be utilized on other robots such as slugs, worms, and snakes. The theoretical model has the potential to be expanded into a more complex model, which could be applied to a robot with multiple segments. Moreover, we observed that the eel-inspired movement, which is primarily based on undulatory movements, resulted in lower peaks in comparison to other movements, which could be beneficial in navigating through tight spaces. This research was funded by an LSRF grant. Kevin Myers was also supported by an Ingram Scholarship. In the context of fluid dynamics, helicity serves as a measure of fluid motion's rotational characteristics, and it remains unchanged over time in certain flow configurations. This study generates helicity's associated conservation law analytically for the compressible Euler equations, thereby providing a solid foundation for investigating helicity's properties in this context. Moreover, our findings can be extended to verify conservation laws for the barotropic compressible Euler equations under specific spatial boundary conditions. However, in scenarios lacking these constraints, numerical approximations reveal that barotropic flows may still preserve helicity, albeit under specific conditions. Further study is required to explore the reasons behind this phenomenon. Finally, our analysis also covers the verification of helicity's conservation for incompressible flows, a scenario that has been well-studied previously in the past. This paper presents helicity's conservation as a crucial element in evaluating numerical models' accuracy and as a valuable tool for better understanding complex rotational fluid motions. In addition, helicity's analytical expression may also serve as a benchmark for comparing and evaluating high-precision numerical models, particularly in scenarios where flows exhibit intricate rotation patterns. This study provides accurate predictions for the remaining eccentricity of binary black hole inspirals when detected through gravitational waves, specifically by LIGO and VIRGO detectors. Using post-Newtonian theory, we've developed formulas that predict the eccentricity at the point of detection, and subsequently, the orbital radius. Our results account for the effects of gravitational waves on inspiral, and we've incorporated limitations imposed by threshold levels of signal-to-noise ratio. We've examined a range of orbital configurations and found that at the point of detection, approximately 26% of inspirals will have an eccentricity greater than 0.1, and 3% will have an eccentricity greater than 0.1 for events with masses greater than 30 solar masses. Our study has enabled the creation of more accurate distributions of remaining eccentricity as a function of mass for binary black hole inspirals, and these distributions can be utilized to model the characteristics of future gravitational wave datasets. Furthermore, we've developed predictions for the effects of gravitational waves on the parameters of binary black hole systems, and we've made recommendations for incorporating these effects into the analysis of GW Catalog data. Experimental findings confirm this prediction. The predicted results were determined using an analytical model based on the principles of electromechanical coupling and the characteristics of each material's harmonic vibration. The close proximity of the materials causes significant mechanical and electrical interactions, resulting in the transient formation of polarizations in each material, facilitated by the electromechanical coupling effect. This interactions enables the efficient transfer of energy between the materials. The degree of coupling between the harmonic vibration of one material and another material's motion can be exploited to improve the transmission of acoustic signals. The total acoustic signal loss is primarily attributed to the boundary conditions and the materials' different properties, rather than their spatial arrangement. The identification of grains larger than typically found elsewhere is key to comprehending the transition from temperate to scorching climates on planets with properties similar to K2-22 b. Ground based telescopes are capable of detecting these larger grains better than space-based ones by measuring the Carina variable star's effect on the system via optical spectral features. Analysis of data generated through the Laser Guide Star Adaptive Optics system on the Large Binocular Telescope reveals the presence of these grains by identifying a shift in the star's color and feature blurring. To account for the data's imperfect precision, a probabilistic method is applied, confirming the need to incorporate larger grains in the model to fit the observed redness. To cause this redness, the model requires a heightened mass loss rate from K2-22 b, suggesting its atmosphere is prone to volatiles evaporation and the formation of a halo around the planet. This is consistent with theory predicting massive grain formation under such conditions and could lead to the grains transferring to the surrounding atmosphere, potentially halting the planet's starlight powered heat exchange within a certain radius of the planet's shadow. This is the first time the mass loss rate has been measured in a gas giant planet like K2-22 b, offering a fresh perspective on its atmosphere loss processes. Moreover, the researched grains are detected during the planet's close approach to its host star, suggesting its atmosphere is experiencing the full effect of volatiles evaporation and grain formation, a phenomenon not seen in less scorching exoplanets. The data from this research is used to develop a model of grain growth, suggesting a brief grain lifespan of around 1.7 hours, to be replaced by smaller grains, re forming the basis for a volatile and dynamic atmosphere of K2-22 b. This research offers a key insight into the volatile and dynamic atmosphere of K2-22 b, a planet with properties similar to those needed for a habitable zone transition. The data from this research could be used in up and coming missions such as the James Webb Space Telescope to identify the planatary atmosphere's property changes and offer a fresh perspective on its atmosphere evolution. This research holds a positive outlook on how ground based telescopes can improve our comprehension of planetary atmosphere loss and grain formation. This condition is fulfilled in numerous significant contexts, including varieties of type $V$, which encompass toric varieties, and complete intersections. The demonstration relies on a previously undiscovered theorem regarding coherent Milnor algebras in the context of toric varieties. Additionally, we establish a novel theorem linking the flatness of the critical set to the cohomology of the Milnor fiber via a generalization of a theorem initially proposed by Teissier. This generalized theorem encompasses a previously established result by Teissier's co-discoverer, Goresky and MacPherson, for singularities with a substantial moduli deficit. The proof involves combining Le Calvez's descent theorem, an analysis of the fiber's cohomology in relation to the Lê residues, and an argument originally proposed by Teissier. Furthermore, we compute the cohomology of the Milnor fiber for a specific family of singularities, establishing that the cohomology exhibits rationality and dimensionality increments that can be calculated. In a related study, we investigate the diophantine analog of this question and demonstrate the coherence of the Milnor fiber in the context of complex hypersurfaces, which has a significant connection to Néron models and the coherence of the special fiber of a semistable reduction. I show how Galileo's mechanical universe, conceived through mathematics, diverges from the philosophical ideals presented in his earlier work, particularly those rooted in Plato's theory of forms. While mathematics allows for accurate predictions, it falls short of addressing deeper, metaphysical concerns that ultimately led Galileo to adopt an empirical approach, prioritizing observation over philosophical speculation in his later scientific work. Just as ignorance has a classifiable structure, I argue that ignorance can also be a product of knowledge, specifically mathematical knowledge, and demonstrate this type of ignorance through the term "Galileo's Blind Spot." Through an examination of his contributions to the scientific revolution, I illustrate the intricate relationship between different forms of ignorance that have far-reaching implications for contemporary discourse in fields like AI, philosophy, and science. This study seeks to reinterpret Galileo's story as a paradigm for the complex interplay between various forms of ignorance that gives rise to new knowledge. Finally, I suggest that this paradigm can be applied to confront the uncertainties surrounding AI, particularly the prospect of superintelligence. In contrast to prevailing narratives emphasizing the dangers of uncontrolled progress, I propose a more nuanced view that highlights the opportunities for growth enabled by the recognition of ignorance, whether inherent or spawned by knowledge. This study is part of a broader effort to chart a course for the future, taking into account the limitations of present understanding, and specifically the Blind Spot represented by Galileo's mathematical universe. In this spirit, I build upon the work of Campanella, Descartes, Hobbes, and Spinoza, whose philosophical ideas, though critiquing Galileo, ultimately led to a comprehensive worldview and a more optimistic view of the future, one that is likely to emerge from the recognition of ignorance surrounding superintelligence. That view, I believe, is a future worth envisioning. In contrast to the conventional focus on the dark implications of ignorance, I this study explores the dark hypothesis as a catalyst for progress, positivity, and a more hopeful future, one that is built on a more complete understanding of the ignorance surrounding the prospect of superintelligence. While the prospect of a superintelligent AI may seem daunting, I this study explores the potential for a brighter future, one enabled by the recognition of ignorance and a more comprehensive understanding of the benefits and challenges posed by the emergence of superintelligence. In contrast to the prevailing views on the risks of uncontrolled progress, this study offers a more optimistic outlook, one that is grounded in the philosophy of Campanella, Descartes, Hobbes, and Spinoza

We introduce a novel technique in automatic program transformation, namely 'Scribe', where the programmer serves as a mere apprentice to a well-defined transformation framework. This involves the programmer merely describing the desired final program using the 'Scribe' language, with the rest of the transformation process being handled automatically by 'Scribe'. For practical purposes, we have developed a specific 'Scribe' language tailored to generating trainee programs in the 'CodeBERT' space. Through our analysis on a range of tasks, we find that 'Scribe' achieves a success rate of 87.4%, significantly outperforming existing program synthesis methods with a 42% improvement in efficiency. Ultimately, we find that 'Scribe' generates more reliable and efficient code compared to traditional programming efforts. The source code for 'Scribe' is openly available on GitHub at the link provided in the reference section. This research builds upon previous studies on program synthesis, template-based programming, and intelligent assistance, contributing novel insights in these areas that were missing from prior research. Additionally, the associated dataset containing automatic translations, as well as a range of tasks is openly made available on GitHub at the link provided in the reference section for the purpose of supporting future research in program synthesis. This research aims to stimulate future studies on program synthesis by providing a range of new tasks and a substantial dataset of automatic translations. Moreover, we have developed a web-based interface for 'Scribe' that can be accessed at the link provided in the reference section for the purpose of enabling other programmers to test the effectiveness of 'Scribe' in their own coding endeavors. This research presents a novel concept in software development that utilizes program transformation to facilitate easier coding efforts for programmers. We describe a trainee program that undergoes these transformations with the ultimate goal of reaching a final, improved version of the program. This research is centered around the underlying mechanism of these transformations, which we term the 'Scribe' framework. We have developed a specific 'Scribe' language, tailored to our dataset, which we find achieves a high success rate in program synthesis. This research is unique in that it explores the application of program transformation in software development, providing a new perspective on this topic. Moreover, we find that 'Scribe' outperforms other program synthesis methods in both efficiency and reliability. This research aims to stimulate future studies on program transformation by providing new insights and applications in software development.
